paye-calculator.notesTitle: 2026 Kenya PAYE, SHA, NSSF Year 4 & Housing Levy Statutory Guide
overview: Pay As You Earn (PAYE) is Kenya's statutory method of deducting income tax at source from employment emoluments under the Income Tax Act (Cap 470) as amended by the Finance Act 2023 and the Tax Laws (Amendment) Act, 2024. Every Kenyan employer is legally required to compute and remit PAYE, Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF/SHA), National Social Security Fund (NSSF), and the Affordable Housing Levy (AHL) on or before the 9th day of the following month via KRA iTax.

Under the 2026 payroll framework, mandatory employee contributions to NSSF Tier I & II (6% of pensionable pay up to KES 108,000, capped at KES 6,480/month under the Year 4 schedule effective February 2026), SHA/SHIF (2.75% of gross salary), and the Affordable Housing Levy (1.5% of gross salary) are treated as allowable pre-tax deductions before applying the five progressive PAYE tax brackets (10% to 35%) and the KES 2,400 monthly personal tax relief.
howItWorks: Compute mandatory statutory deductions from Gross Salary: NSSF (6% of gross up to KES 108,000 upper earning limit = max KES 6,480), SHA/SHIF (2.75% of gross, min KES 300), and Affordable Housing Levy (1.5% of gross).

Determine Taxable (Chargeable) Pay by subtracting allowable pre-tax deductions (NSSF + SHA/SHIF + Housing Levy + registered pension up to KES 30,000/month + owner-occupied mortgage interest up to KES 30,000/month) from Gross Pay.

Apply progressive KRA monthly PAYE bands to Chargeable Pay: 10% on the first KES 24,000; 25% on the next KES 8,333; 30% on the next KES 467,667; 32.5% on the next KES 300,000; and 35% on any income above KES 800,000.
Subtract Personal Relief (KES 2,400/month) and any eligible insurance relief (15% of premiums up to KES 5,000/month) from Gross Tax to arrive at Net PAYE Payable and Net Take-Home Pay.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: KES 100,000 Monthly Gross Salary in 2026
workedExample.scenario: An employee in Nairobi earns a gross monthly salary of KES 100,000 with no additional voluntary pension or mortgage deductions:
steps: NSSF Year 4 Deduction (6% of KES 100,000): KES 6,000.00 (Tier I: KES 540 + Tier II: KES 5,460)
SHA / SHIF Contribution (2.75% of KES 100,000): KES 2,750.00
Affordable Housing Levy (1.5% of KES 100,000): KES 1,500.00
Net PAYE After Personal Relief: KES 21,708.35 − KES 2,400 = KES 19,308.35
workedExample.takeaway: Because SHA (2.75%) and Housing Levy (1.5%) are pre-tax allowable deductions, they reduce chargeable pay by KES 4,250 and save the employee KES 1,275 in monthly PAYE.

complianceTips: Employers must remit PAYE, Affordable Housing Levy, and NITA (KES 50/employee) via KRA iTax by the 9th of every month to avoid the 5% late payment penalty and 1% monthly interest.
Employees earning KES 24,000 or less pay KES 0 net PAYE because the KES 2,400 personal relief fully offsets the 10% tax on the first band.
When negotiating an employment offer phrased in 'Net Take-Home Pay', switch to our Reverse (Net → Gross) tab to compute the exact gross contract figure required.
notes: Enter your monthly or annual gross salary (KES) and optional pension or mortgage interest deductions to calculate your exact 2026 net take-home pay.

View a complete statutory payslip breakdown including NSSF Tier I & II (6% up to KES 108,000 pensionable pay, max KES 6,480), Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF/SHA at 2.75% of gross), Affordable Housing Levy (1.5% of gross), taxable pay after allowable pre-tax deductions, progressive PAYE bands (10% to 35%), and KES 2,400 monthly personal relief.
Formulas strictly implement the Income Tax Act (Cap 470), Tax Laws (Amendment) Act 2024, NSSF Act 2013 (Year 4 schedule), and Social Health Insurance Act.

faq.question: What PAYE tax bands apply in Kenya?
faq.answer: Kenya uses progressive tax bands: 10% for the first KES 24,000, 25% for KES 24,001–32,333, 30% for KES 32,334–500,000, 32.5% for KES 500,001–800,000, and 35% above KES 800,000. A personal relief of KES 2,400 per month is applied.

faq.question: Is the Affordable Housing Levy mandatory?
faq.answer: Yes, since the Finance Act 2023 and the Supreme Court ruling upholding it, all employed persons pay 1.5% of gross salary as the Affordable Housing Levy. The employer also contributes 1.5%. Under the Tax Laws (Amendment) Act, 2024, the employee's Housing Levy and SHIF contributions are full pre-tax allowable deductions.

faq.question: What are the new NSSF rates in Kenya?
faq.answer: Under the NSSF Act 2013 (now in effect), employees contribute 6% of pensionable pay. Under the Year 4 schedule (effective February 2026), Tier I covers up to KES 9,000 (max KES 540) and Tier II covers KES 9,001–108,000 (max KES 5,940; total max KES 6,480/month). The employer matches these contributions.

faq.question: How is SHA calculated in Kenya?
faq.answer: The Social Health Insurance Fund contribution is calculated at 2.75% of gross salary and is remitted through the Social Health Authority. It replaced the former NHIF income bands.

faq.question: Does this calculator include the Housing Levy tax relief?
faq.answer: Yes. The employee's Housing Levy contribution qualifies as tax relief, which effectively reduces your PAYE. This calculator applies that relief automatically to give you the most accurate net pay figure.

mpesa-fee-calculator.notesTitle: Safaricom M-Pesa Tariff Schedule & Fee Optimization Guide (2026)
overview: Safaricom's M-Pesa platform processes over 90% of mobile money transactions in Kenya across person-to-person transfers, M-Pesa Agent cash withdrawals, Lipa na M-Pesa Buy Goods tills, and PayBill business collections. Each transaction tier between KES 1 and KES 250,000 is governed by Safaricom's published consumer tariff schedule approved by the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK).

Understanding the exact step boundaries between M-Pesa tariff bands allows consumers and SME owners to avoid overpaying on transfers, determine the exact amount to send when covering the recipient's withdrawal fee ('tuma na ya kutoa'), and identify when splitting a transaction saves money.
howItWorks: Select your transaction type: Send to Registered M-Pesa User, Send to Unregistered / Other Network, Withdraw from M-Pesa Agent, or ATM Withdrawal.
Enter any transaction amount between KES 1 and KES 250,000 (the maximum single-transaction CBK limit).
Toggle 'Include Agent Withdrawal Fee' to compute the exact total amount you must send so the recipient walks away with the full net cash after paying the agent.
Review the Smart Split Optimizer, which automatically checks whether splitting your transfer into two smaller bands reduces total transaction fees.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Sending KES 10,000 'Na Ya Kutoa' (With Withdrawal Fee)
workedExample.scenario: You want a recipient to withdraw exactly KES 10,000 cash at an M-Pesa agent:
steps: Standard M-Pesa Agent Withdrawal Fee for the KES 7,501 – 10,000 band: KES 115
However, if you send KES 10,115, the recipient's withdrawal amount crosses into the KES 10,001 – 15,000 band, where the agent withdrawal fee jumps to KES 167!
Therefore, to cover the higher band withdrawal fee so the recipient nets KES 10,000 cash, you must send KES 10,167 (plus KES 90 sending fee = KES 10,257 total cost).
workedExample.takeaway: Crossing a tariff band boundary (such as KES 2,500, KES 3,500, KES 5,000, KES 7,500, or KES 10,000) when adding withdrawal fees jumps the agent fee to the next bracket—our calculator solves this boundary jump automatically.

complianceTips: Transfers of KES 100 and below to registered users are 100% free (KES 0 sending fee).
Maximum M-Pesa account balance is KES 500,000 and maximum daily transaction limit is KES 500,000 (up to KES 250,000 per single transaction).
Lipa na M-Pesa Buy Goods (Till Number) payments are generally free for consumers, whereas PayBill charges depend on whether the merchant uses a customer-pays or business-pays tariff.
notes: Enter any transaction amount between KES 1 and KES 250,000 and select the transaction type (Send to M-Pesa, Send to Unregistered/Other Network, Withdraw at Agent, or ATM Withdrawal) to calculate exact Safaricom M-Pesa charges.
Compare single-transfer fees against split-transaction strategies and review daily transaction limits (KES 500,000/day, KES 250,000 per single transaction).
Tariff brackets reflect the current published Safaricom PLC M-Pesa consumer tariff schedule.

faq.question: Are M-Pesa Buy Goods (Lipa Na M-Pesa) transactions free?
faq.answer: Yes, Safaricom does not charge customers any fee for Buy Goods (till number) transactions. This makes Lipa Na M-Pesa the cheapest way to pay for goods and services.

faq.question: How much does M-Pesa charge to send money?
faq.answer: M-Pesa charges vary by amount and whether the recipient is registered. Sending to a registered user ranges from KES 0 (for amounts under KES 100) to KES 108 (for amounts over KES 25,000). Sending to unregistered users costs more.

faq.question: What is the M-Pesa maximum transaction limit?
faq.answer: The maximum single M-Pesa transaction is KES 250,000. The maximum daily transaction total is KES 500,000, and the maximum M-Pesa account balance is KES 500,000.

faq.question: Is receiving money on M-Pesa free?
faq.answer: Yes, receiving money on M-Pesa is always free regardless of the amount. You only pay fees when sending money or withdrawing.

faq.question: How can I save on M-Pesa fees?
faq.answer: Use Buy Goods (Lipa Na M-Pesa) whenever possible as it's free. When sending money, check the fee boundaries — sometimes sending KES 500 instead of KES 501 can save you fees because of tariff band transitions.

sacco-chama-calculator.notesTitle: SASRA Tier-1 SACCO Loan Multiplier, Reducing Balance & Dividend Guide
overview: Deposit-Taking SACCOs (DT-SACCOs) regulated by the SACCO Societies Regulatory Authority (SASRA) under the SACCO Societies Act (Cap 490B) are the backbone of household credit and wealth accumulation in Kenya. Unlike commercial banks that price personal loans at 16%–22% p.a. based on CBK's base rate and risk margins, Back Office Service Activity (BOSA) SACCO loans typically charge a capped 12% per annum (1% per month) on a reducing-balance basis.

Members qualify for development and emergency loans based on a deposit multiplier—typically 3x, 4x, or 5x their non-withdrawable BOSA share deposits—secured by co-guarantors within the SACCO, while continuing to earn annual interest rebates (9%–13%) on their deposits and dividends (12%–20%) on share capital.
howItWorks: Select a benchmark SASRA Tier-1 SACCO (such as Mwalimu National, Stima, Kenya National Police, Harambee, Tower, Afya, Unaitas, or Waumini) or enter custom rates.
Enter your accumulated BOSA non-withdrawable deposits and core share capital to compute your maximum 3x/4x/5x loan eligibility and required guarantor gap.
Compare monthly amortization payments and total interest payable under the standard 12% p.a. SACCO reducing-balance formula against a commercial bank loan over 12 to 84 months.
Calculate your net annual cash payout after statutory 5% Withholding Tax (WHT) on SACCO dividends and deposit rebates.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: KES 500,000 BOSA Deposits & KES 1.5M Loan Over 48 Months
workedExample.scenario: A SACCO member has KES 500,000 in BOSA deposits and KES 40,000 in core share capital at a SACCO offering a 3x multiplier, 11% deposit rebate, and 15% share dividend:
steps: Maximum BOSA Loan Limit (3× multiplier): KES 500,000 × 3 = KES 1,500,000
Required Guarantor Coverage: KES 1,500,000 − KES 500,000 (own deposits) = KES 1,000,000 from fellow SACCO guarantors
Monthly Repayment at 12% p.a. Reducing Balance (48 months): KES 39,501/month (Total interest: KES 396,036)
Commercial Bank Equivalent at 18.5% p.a. (48 months): KES 44,415/month (Total interest: KES 631,920 — SACCO saves KES 235,884!)
Annual Gross Rebates & Dividends: (500,000 × 11% = 55,000) + (40,000 × 15% = 6,000) = KES 61,000 gross (KES 57,950 net after 5% WHT)
workedExample.takeaway: Even while servicing a BOSA loan, your locked deposits continue earning annual rebates that offset nearly 60% of your effective annual loan interest cost.

complianceTips: Always verify that a SACCO is officially licensed by SASRA (sasra.go.ke) before depositing funds; SASRA publishes the authorized list of DT-SACCOs and NWDT-SACCOs annually in the Kenya Gazette.
Under the Income Tax Act, qualifying dividends and interest rebates paid by registered SACCOs to resident members attract a final 5% Withholding Tax deducted at source.
Under Kenya's one-third (1/3) basic salary rule (Employment Act Section 19), total payroll deductions including SACCO loans cannot leave an employee with less than one-third of their basic wage.
notes: Model your Deposit-Taking SACCO (DT-SACCO) or registered Chama savings growth, BOSA loan multiplier (3x to 4x deposits), monthly reducing-balance loan repayments, and annual dividend/rebate payouts.
Account for the 5% statutory Withholding Tax (WHT) on SACCO dividends and interest on deposits, and compare effective net borrowing costs after annual deposit rebates.
Benchmarks reflect SACCO Societies Regulatory Authority (SASRA) supervision reports and standard Kenyan cooperative lending terms.

faq.question: What is the difference between SACCO Dividends and Interest on Deposits (Rebates)?
faq.answer: Dividends are paid on permanent, non-withdrawable Share Capital (typically 12%–20%), while Interest on Deposits (Rebates) is paid on monthly BOSA deposits (typically 9%–13%) weighted by how many months each deposit stayed in the SACCO.

faq.question: Why is a reducing-balance SACCO loan cheaper than a flat-rate loan?
faq.answer: At 1% per month on a reducing balance (12% p.a.), interest is charged only on the remaining principal each month—equivalent to roughly 6.5% flat rate per year.

faq.question: How is the 12% p.a. (1% per month) SACCO reducing-balance loan interest calculated?
faq.answer: Unlike flat-rate loans where interest is charged on the original principal throughout the loan term, SASRA-regulated BOSA loans charge 1% per month strictly on the remaining unpaid principal balance each month, making total interest roughly half that of a 12% flat-rate loan.

faq.question: What is the difference between BOSA Dividends on Share Capital and Interest Rebates on Deposits?
faq.answer: Share Capital is permanent equity that earns an annual Dividend rate (typically 12%–20% in Tier-1 SACCOs) and cannot be withdrawn when leaving the SACCO (only transferred to another member), whereas BOSA Non-Withdrawable Deposits back your 3x/4x loan multiplier, earn an annual Interest Rebate (typically 9%–13%), and are refundable after a 60-day written notice if you have no outstanding loans or guarantor commitments.

faq.question: Are SACCO dividends and interest rebates subject to KRA Withholding Tax?
faq.answer: Yes. Under the Income Tax Act (Cap 470), SACCO dividends on share capital and interest rebates on member deposits for resident individuals are subject to a 5% statutory Withholding Tax deducted at source before payout to your FOSA account.

helb-calculator.notesTitle: HELB Student Loan Repayment, Interest & Clearance Guide
overview: The Higher Education Loans Board (HELB), established under the HELB Act (Cap 213A), finances undergraduate, postgraduate, and TVET students across Kenya. Undergraduate loans accrue interest at 4% per annum (plus a KES 1,000 annual ledger maintenance fee) and enter mandatory repayment one year after completion of studies or immediately upon formal employment.

Employers are legally obligated under Section 15 of the HELB Act to deduct monthly repayments from employees' salaries and remit them by the 15th of the following month. Loan accounts that remain unpaid without formal deferment after the grace period attract a statutory KES 5,000 per month default penalty.
howItWorks: Enter your total principal borrowed across your study years, graduation year, and current gross monthly salary.
The calculator models accrued 4% annual simple interest during your post-graduation period and estimates your required monthly payroll deduction.
Review the full year-by-year amortization schedule showing how each monthly payment splits between 4% interest, ledger fees, and principal reduction until your balance reaches KES 0.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: KES 200,000 HELB Principal Over 4 University Years
workedExample.scenario: A graduate borrowed KES 50,000 per year for 4 years (KES 200,000 principal) and begins repaying KES 4,500 per month two years after graduation:
steps: Accrued Interest & Ledger Fees Prior to Repayment: Approx. KES 18,000 (bringing starting balance to ~KES 218,000)
Monthly Interest Accrual at 4% p.a.: ~KES 727/month initially, declining as principal is paid down
Projected Payoff Timeline at KES 4,500/month: Approximately 53 months (4.4 years)
Total Interest Paid Over Loan Life: Approx. KES 21,500
workedExample.takeaway: Increasing your voluntary monthly HELB payment by just KES 1,500/month via M-Pesa PayBill 200800 cuts over 14 months off your repayment timeline.

complianceTips: If you are unemployed after the 1-year grace period, submit a formal loan deferment request on the HELB portal (helb.co.ke) to avoid the KES 5,000 monthly default penalty.
Once your loan is fully repaid, apply for your official HELB Clearance Certificate via eCitizen/HELB portal—issuance is free for loanees who have cleared their balances.
Watch for periodic HELB 80%–100% penalty waiver amnesties if your account has accumulated historical default fines.
notes: Enter your total Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) principal loan balance, applicable annual interest rate (typically 4% p.a. for undergraduate loans), and monthly repayment amount.
Calculate your exact payoff duration in months and years, total cumulative interest payable, and month-by-month amortization schedule.
Under the HELB Act, statutory employer deductions begin after the 1-year post-graduation grace period; voluntary lump-sum payments directly reduce principal and total interest.

faq.question: What is the HELB loan interest rate?
faq.answer: HELB charges 4% per annum simple interest on the outstanding loan balance. Interest starts accruing from the date of first disbursement, not from when you start repaying.

faq.question: When do I start repaying my HELB loan?
faq.answer: You get a 1-year grace period after completing your studies. After that, repayment begins. Your employer is required by law to deduct HELB payments from your salary.

faq.question: What is the minimum HELB monthly repayment?
faq.answer: The minimum is KES 1,500 per month or 10% of your gross salary, whichever is higher. Making higher payments reduces your total interest and shortens the repayment period.

faq.question: What happens if I don't repay my HELB loan?
faq.answer: HELB can list you with credit reference bureaus (CRB), preventing you from accessing other credit. A 5% late penalty is also charged on the outstanding amount. HELB can also pursue legal action.

faq.question: Can I make lump sum payments to HELB?
faq.answer: Yes, HELB accepts lump sum payments which reduce the principal amount. This is recommended to cut down on total interest paid and shorten the repayment period.

stamp-duty-calculator.notesTitle: Kenya Land Transfer, Stamp Duty (Cap 480) & LSK Conveyancing Fee Guide
overview: Purchasing land, a residential house, or commercial property in Kenya involves statutory transaction costs beyond the agreed purchase price. Under the Stamp Duty Act (Cap 480), the buyer must pay Stamp Duty assessed on the higher of the contract price or the Government Chief Valuer's open-market valuation before the title deed can be transferred on the Ardhisasa digital land registry.

In addition to Stamp Duty (4% for urban/municipality land and 2% for rural agricultural land), buyers must budget for legal conveyancing fees regulated by the Advocates Remuneration Order (Cap 16), official title search fees, valuation fees, and consent-to-transfer fees.
howItWorks: Enter the property purchase price or Chief Government Valuer assessment in KES.
Select the property classification: Urban / Municipality (4% Stamp Duty) or Rural / Agricultural Land (2% Stamp Duty).
Toggle the First-Time Homebuyer / Affordable Housing Scheme exemption if purchasing an approved unit exempt under the Stamp Duty Act.
Review the itemized cost breakdown covering Stamp Duty, LSK Advocates Remuneration Order scale fees, 16% VAT on legal services, and Ardhisasa registration disbursements.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Buying a KES 8,000,000 Residential Plot in Nairobi (Urban 4%)
workedExample.scenario: A buyer purchases a quarter-acre residential plot within Nairobi Municipality valued at KES 8,000,000:
steps: Urban Stamp Duty (4% of KES 8,000,000): KES 320,000
LSK Statutory Conveyancing Scale Fee (~1.5%–2% tiered scale): ~KES 135,000
16% VAT on Advocate Legal Fees: KES 21,600
Official Search, Valuation, Clearance & Registration Disbursements: ~KES 15,000
Total Closing Costs Above Purchase Price: ~KES 491,600 (6.15% of property value)
workedExample.takeaway: Buyers of urban property in Kenya should always budget an extra 5.5% to 6.5% above the purchase price to cover Stamp Duty, legal fees, and registration costs.

complianceTips: Stamp Duty must be paid within 30 days of execution of the transfer instrument (for documents executed within Kenya) to avoid a 5% penalty for every quarter in default.
Transfers of rural agricultural land require mandatory Land Control Board (LCB) consent within 6 months of the sale agreement under the Land Control Act (Cap 302).
Transfers between spouses or to a family trust / family company meeting statutory conditions qualify for specific Stamp Duty exemptions.
notes: Enter the property purchase price or government valuation and select the location category (Urban/Municipality at 4% vs. Rural/Agricultural at 2%) to calculate Stamp Duty payable on land transfers in Kenya.
Include advocate legal fee estimates under the Advocates (Remuneration) Order, valuation fees, and Ardhisasa/land registry registration charges to budget your total property closing cost.
Rates follow the Stamp Duty Act (Cap 480) and Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) iTax property transfer guidelines.

faq.question: What is stamp duty in Kenya?
faq.answer: Stamp duty is a government tax charged on the transfer of property (land or buildings) in Kenya. It is payable to the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) within 30 days of executing the transfer instrument.

faq.question: What is the stamp duty rate for urban vs rural property?
faq.answer: Stamp duty is 4% of the market value for urban and peri-urban properties, and 2% for rural properties. First-time buyers under the Affordable Housing Fund (AHF) scheme are fully exempt.

faq.question: What are conveyancing fees in Kenya?
faq.answer: Conveyancing fees are legal fees paid to an advocate for handling the property transfer process. Rates are set by the Law Society of Kenya (LSK) Advocates Remuneration Order on a progressive scale based on property value.

faq.question: Are first-time home buyers exempt from stamp duty?
faq.answer: Yes. Under the Affordable Housing Fund (AHF) scheme introduced in Finance Act 2023, first-time buyers of affordable housing units are exempt from stamp duty entirely.

faq.question: What other costs are involved in property transfer?
faq.answer: Beyond stamp duty and conveyancing fees, you may also need to pay: Land Registry registration fee (KES 5,000 flat), search fee (KES 520), consent to transfer (KES 5,000), valuation fee (~0.25% of property value), and county-specific land rates clearance.

vehicle-insurance-calculator.notesTitle: IRA Kenya Motor Insurance Minimum Premiums, TPO & Comprehensive Guide
overview: Under the Insurance (Motor Vehicles Third Party Risks) Act (Cap 405), every motor vehicle operating on Kenyan public roads must carry valid insurance covering third-party bodily injury and death. The Insurance Regulatory Authority (IRA) sets minimum premium guidelines across Private, Commercial (Own Goods / General Cartage), Public Service Vehicles (PSV), and Motorcycles (Boda Boda).

In addition to basic base premiums, motor policies in Kenya are subject to three mandatory statutory levies: Policyholders Compensation Fund (PCF at 0.25%), Insurance Training Levy (ITL at 0.20%), and KES 40 Stamp Duty per policy certificate.
howItWorks: Select your vehicle class (Private Car, Commercial Vehicle, PSV Matatu/Taxi, or Motorcycle) and enter the current market / insured value in KES.
Compare Third-Party Only (TPO) statutory annual premiums against Comprehensive coverage rates (typically 3.5%–6.0% of sum insured).
Toggle optional extensions such as Political Violence & Terrorism (PVT), Excess Protector, Windscreen cover, and Courtesy Car to calculate your exact total policy outlay including IRA levies.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Comprehensive Cover for a KES 1,800,000 Private Car
workedExample.scenario: Insuring a private saloon car valued at KES 1,800,000 under a 4.0% Comprehensive policy with Excess Protector (0.25%) and PVT (0.25%):
steps: Base Comprehensive Premium (4.0% of KES 1,800,000): KES 72,000
Excess Protector (0.25%) + PVT Extension (0.25%): KES 4,500 + KES 4,500 = KES 9,000
Subtotal Premium: KES 81,000
IRA Statutory Levies (0.25% PCF + 0.20% ITL = 0.45%): KES 364.50 + KES 40 Stamp Duty
Total Annual Payable Premium: KES 81,404.50 (vs. ~KES 7,500/year for Third-Party Only)
workedExample.takeaway: For vehicles older than 12 years or valued under KES 600,000, many underwriters apply minimum comprehensive premium floors (KES 30,000–37,500) or recommend Third-Party Fire & Theft.

complianceTips: Verify that your digital motor insurance certificate is genuine by dialing the Association of Kenya Insurers (AKI) USSD code or checking the IRA portal.
Never insure a vehicle below its actual market value—if you under-insure by 30%, insurers apply the 'Average Clause' and reduce any claim payout by 30%.
Comprehensive policies typically stop covering vehicles older than 12–15 years without a mechanical valuation report from an approved assessor (e.g., AA Kenya or Regent).
notes: Enter your vehicle's current market value (KES), usage class (Private Car, Commercial Own Goods, PSV Matatu/Chauffeured, or Motorcycle), and coverage type (Comprehensive vs. Third Party Only) to estimate annual motor insurance premiums.

See itemized statutory levies included in Kenyan policies: Insurance Training Levy (0.2%), Policyholders Compensation Fund (PCF 0.25%), and KES 40 Stamp Duty, plus optional Excess Protector and Political Violence & Terrorism (PVT) riders.
Rate benchmarks follow Insurance Regulatory Authority (IRA) guidelines and Cap 405 compulsory third-party motor insurance requirements.

faq.question: Is vehicle insurance mandatory in Kenya?
faq.answer: Yes. Third Party Only insurance is the minimum legal requirement under the Insurance (Motor Vehicle Third Party Risks) Act (Cap 405). Driving without valid insurance is a criminal offence with a fine of up to KES 100,000 or imprisonment.

faq.question: What is the minimum car insurance cost in Kenya?
faq.answer: The minimum Third Party Only insurance for a private vehicle is KES 7,500 per year. This covers injury/death to third parties and damage to third party property, but does not cover your own vehicle.

faq.question: What is the difference between Third Party and Comprehensive insurance?
faq.answer: Third Party Only covers damage to other people and their property. Comprehensive cover additionally protects your own vehicle against damage, theft, fire, and windscreen breakage. Comprehensive premiums are typically 4–6% of your vehicle's value.

faq.question: Who sets minimum insurance premiums in Kenya?
faq.answer: The Insurance Regulatory Authority (IRA) sets minimum premium rates for all motor insurance categories. Actual premiums from insurance companies may be higher based on the insurer's risk assessment and your driving history.

faq.question: Do boda bodas need insurance?
faq.answer: Yes. Motorcycles (including boda bodas) require at least Third Party Only insurance with a minimum premium of KES 4,000/year. This is enforced by NTSA and traffic police.

cbc-curriculum.notesTitle: KICD CBC Curriculum (2-6-3-3-3), Senior School Pathways & Grade-Age Guide
overview: Kenya's Competency-Based Curriculum (CBC), designed by the Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) under the Basic Education Curriculum Framework (BECF), replaced the exam-centric 8-4-4 system with a 2-6-3-3-3 progression: 2 years of Pre-Primary (PP1–PP2), 6 years of Primary (Grades 1–6), 3 years of Junior School (Grades 7–9), 3 years of Senior School (Grades 10–12), and 3+ years of University or TVET tertiary education.

Following the Presidential Working Party on Education Reforms (PWPER) recommendations implemented by the Ministry of Education, learning areas were rationalized to reduce workload while preserving seven core competencies: Communication & Collaboration, Critical Thinking & Problem Solving, Creativity & Imagination, Citizenship, Digital Literacy, Learning to Learn, and Self-Efficacy.
howItWorks: Select any CBC tier (Pre-Primary, Lower Primary, Upper Primary, Junior School, or Senior School) to inspect official KICD learning areas and subject descriptions.
Review the three Senior School (Grades 10–12) career pathways—STEM, Social Sciences, and Arts & Sports Science—along with core and elective subject tracks.
Use the integrated 2026 Birth-Year & Grade-Age Calculator to check which CBC grade your child belongs in and compare it against the former 8-4-4 Standard/Form equivalent.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Senior School Placement & Pathway Selection (Grade 9 → Grade 10)
workedExample.scenario: A learner born in 2011 completes Grade 9 (Junior School) and sits the Kenya Junior School Education Assessment (KJSEA):
steps: Cumulative Placement Score: 20% from Grade 6 KPSEA + 20% from Junior School SBA (Grades 7–9) + 60% from Grade 9 summative KJSEA
Pathway Selection: The learner selects 1 of 3 pathways (60% of Senior School slots are allocated to STEM, 25% to Social Sciences, and 15% to Arts & Sports Science)

Senior School Subjects (Grades 10–12): Every learner takes 4 compulsory core subjects (English, Kiswahili/KSL, Community Service Learning, Physical Education) plus 3 pathway electives (7 subjects total)
workedExample.takeaway: Continuous School-Based Assessments (SBAs) in Grades 4–9 account for 40% of a student's Senior School placement weight—consistent coursework matters as much as final exams.

complianceTips: Every learner must have a valid NEMIS (National Education Management Information System) / KNEC Assessment Number from PP1/Grade 1 to track SBA scores across school transfers.
Under MoE age guidelines, a child joins PP1 in the calendar year they turn 4 and Grade 1 in the year they turn 6.
Junior School (Grades 7–9) is domiciled within existing primary schools as a comprehensive school model.
notes: Select any education tier under Kenya's 2-6-3-3-3 Competency-Based Curriculum (Pre-Primary, Lower/Upper Primary, Junior School, or Senior School) to inspect official KICD learning areas.

Review Senior School (Grades 10–12) specialization tracks across STEM, Social Sciences, and Arts & Sports Science alongside KNEC national assessment milestones (KPSEA, KJSEA, and Senior School Assessment).
Curriculum structures reflect the Ministry of Education and Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) 2026 implementation guidelines.

faq.question: What is the CBC education system in Kenya?
faq.answer: The Competency-Based Curriculum (CBC) replaced the 8-4-4 system. It uses a 2-6-3-3-3 structure: 2 years Pre-Primary, 6 years Primary (Lower + Upper), 3 years Junior Secondary, and 3 years Senior Secondary. It focuses on developing competencies rather than rote memorization.

faq.question: What subjects are taught in CBC Kenya?
faq.answer: CBC subjects vary by level. Pre-Primary has Language, Mathematical, Environmental, Psychomotor, and Religious activities. Primary adds English, Kiswahili, Mathematics, Science & Technology, and more. Junior Secondary introduces Integrated Science, Computer Science, and Business Studies.

faq.question: What are the three Senior Secondary pathways?
faq.answer: Grade 10–12 students choose one of three pathways: STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics), Arts & Sports Science (visual/performing arts, sports), or Social Sciences (humanities, business, economics).

faq.question: When did CBC start in Kenya?
faq.answer: CBC was piloted in 2017 and fully rolled out starting 2019 with PP1 and Grade 1. Junior Secondary (Grade 7) began in 2023. Senior Secondary (Grade 10) is being phased in from 2026.

faq.question: What is the equivalent of Form 1 in CBC?
faq.answer: Form 1 in the old 8-4-4 system is roughly equivalent to Grade 9 (JSS 3) in CBC. Grade 7 replaced Standard 7, and the Junior Secondary (JSS) covers what was previously late primary and early secondary.

kuccps-cluster-calculator.notesTitle: KUCCPS 20-Cluster Weighted Formula & University Placement Guide (2026)
overview: The Kenya Universities and Colleges Central Placement Service (KUCCPS), established under Section 55 of the Universities Act (No. 42 of 2012), coordinates government-sponsored student placement into public and private universities, national polytechnics, and TVET institutions. While a minimum KCSE mean grade of C+ (46 points) qualifies a candidate for Bachelor's degree consideration, admission into specific competitive courses is determined by weighted Cluster Points.

KUCCPS groups all university degree programmes into 20 distinct clusters. Each cluster defines four mandatory KCSE subject categories (Subject 1, Subject 2, Subject 3, and Subject 4) that reflect the academic foundation required for that discipline.
howItWorks: Enter your KCSE letter grades (A to E) across the subjects you sat in the national examination.
The calculator evaluates each of the 20 KUCCPS clusters by matching your highest eligible grades to the 4 required cluster subject slots without double-counting any subject.
Compare your resulting cluster weight (out of 48) against historical university cutoff points and inspect the eligible degree programmes in each cluster.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Official KUCCPS Weighted Cluster Formula
workedExample.scenario: A student scores A (12) in Mathematics, A- (11) in Physics, B+ (10) in Chemistry, and A- (11) in English, with a 7-subject KCSE aggregate of 76 out of 84:
steps: Raw Cluster Subject Score (r): 12 + 11 + 10 + 11 = 44 out of 48
Aggregate 7-Subject KCSE Score (t): 76 out of 84
KUCCPS Formula: C = √((r / 48) × (t / 84)) × 48
workedExample.takeaway: Both your 4 core cluster subjects (r) and your overall 7-subject aggregate (t) influence your final KUCCPS cluster points—strong performance in humanities/languages boosts your STEM cluster score.

complianceTips: Always check both the overall Cluster Cutoff and individual Subject Minimums (e.g., B+ in Biology and Chemistry for Medicine) on the official KUCCPS student portal (students.kuccps.net).
Under the New Higher Education Funding Model (HEFM), university placement via KUCCPS is separate from funding—after placement, apply for your scholarship and HELB loan on hef.co.ke.
During First and Second Revision of Choices, avoid placing 4 choices with cutoffs higher than your calculated cluster points.
notes: Enter your KCSE grades in the 4 required cluster subjects plus your overall 8-subject KCSE aggregate points to calculate your weighted KUCCPS cluster score out of 48.
Compare your computed cluster points against recent university degree cutoff thresholds for Medicine, Engineering, Law, Architecture, Computer Science, Nursing, Education, and Business.
Calculations implement the official Kenya Universities and Colleges Central Placement Service (KUCCPS) square-root weighting formula.

faq.question: How are KUCCPS cluster points calculated?
faq.answer: Each university course belongs to a cluster. Each cluster specifies 4 required subjects with weights (typically 2, 1, 0.5, 0.5). Your cluster weight = sum of (Grade points × subject weight). Grade points: A=12, A-=11, B+=10, B=9, down to E=1.

faq.question: What is the maximum cluster weight?
faq.answer: The maximum cluster weight is 48 points (if you score A in all 4 weighted subjects: 12×2 + 12×1 + 12×0.5 + 12×0.5 = 48).

faq.question: How many clusters does KUCCPS have?
faq.answer: KUCCPS has approximately 15-20+ clusters, each representing a group of related university courses. Medicine is Cluster 1, Engineering is Cluster 2, Law is Cluster 10, etc.

faq.question: Do cluster weights change every year?
faq.answer: The cluster composition (which subjects and weights) rarely changes. However, the minimum cut-off points for specific courses at specific universities change annually based on demand and available slots.

faq.question: Can I calculate cluster weights for courses I didn't take?
faq.answer: You can only calculate cluster weight for clusters where you took the required subjects. If a cluster requires Biology but you didn't take it, that cluster won't be applicable to you.

kcse-grade-calculator.notesTitle: KNEC KCSE 8-Subject Mean Grade & Career Eligibility Methodology
overview: The Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE), administered annually by the Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC), grades candidates on a 12-point scale from Grade A (12 points) down to Grade E (1 point). Your overall KCSE Mean Grade determines your eligibility for Bachelor's degrees (C+ and above), TVET/KMTC Diplomas (C plain and C-), Craft Certificates (D+ and D), and entry into regulated professional training such as teaching, nursing, police, and military cadet intakes.

Understanding how KNEC aggregates subject points and maps mean scores to letter grades helps students, parents, and career counselors set realistic subject targets and verify tertiary admission requirements.
howItWorks: Select your letter grades (A to E) for English and at least 7 additional KCSE subjects.
If you enter 9 subjects, the calculator automatically drops the lowest optional subject and sums the best 7 subjects alongside compulsory core subjects.
Total aggregate points are divided by 8 to compute your exact Mean Score (to 2 decimal places) and mapped to the official KNEC letter grade boundary table.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Computing Mean Grade from 8 KCSE Subjects
workedExample.scenario: A candidate scores: English B+ (10), Kiswahili A- (11), Mathematics B+ (10), Biology B (9), Chemistry B+ (10), History A- (11), CRE A (12), and Business Studies B+ (10):
steps: Total Aggregate Points: 10 + 11 + 10 + 9 + 10 + 11 + 12 + 10 = 83 points (out of 96)
Mean Score Calculation: 83 ÷ 8 = 10.375 (rounded to 10.38)
KNEC Grade Boundary Mapping: 9.50 – 10.49 corresponds to Mean Grade B+ (10.50+ is required for A-)
Career Eligibility: Qualifies for direct KUCCPS university degree entry (Engineering, Law, Computer Science, Commerce, Education, Nursing)
workedExample.takeaway: Improving just one subject from B (9) to B+ (10) raises the aggregate from 83 to 84 points (10.50 mean score), crossing the boundary from B+ to A-!

complianceTips: For Teachers Service Commission (TSC) B.Ed. registration, candidates must not only score C+ overall in KCSE but also achieve at least C+ in their two teaching subjects.
Kenya Medical Training College (KMTC) Diploma programmes typically require a minimum C plain overall plus specific C plain grades in English/Kiswahili and Biology.
Official replacement of lost KCSE certificates (Confirmation of Results) is processed exclusively through the KNEC QMIS portal.
notes: Select your letter grades (A to E) across 8 KCSE subjects—including compulsory English—to compute your aggregate KNEC points (out of 84 or 96) and official mean grade.
Review instant eligibility indicators for university degree placement (C+ and above), TVET diploma programmes (C and C-), and artisan/certificate courses.
Grading boundaries follow the Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) 12-point scale.

faq.question: How is the KCSE mean grade calculated?
faq.answer: KNEC takes your 7 best subjects plus English (which is compulsory). The total points from these 8 subjects is divided by 8 to get the mean score, which is then mapped to a letter grade.

faq.question: Is English compulsory in KCSE?
faq.answer: Yes, English is compulsory and must be included in the 8 subjects used for mean grade calculation, regardless of the grade scored.

faq.question: What mean grade do I need for university in Kenya?
faq.answer: The minimum mean grade for university degree programs through KUCCPS is generally C+ (7 points). However, competitive courses like Medicine require A- or A. Diploma courses require C, and certificate courses require C-.

kcse-school-rankings.notesTitle: KCSE Secondary School Performance Metrics & County Benchmarking Guide
overview: Analyzing secondary school performance in the Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) requires looking beyond raw plain-A counts. Because National Schools enrol 400 to 700+ candidates per cohort while Extra-County and Private schools often enrol 80 to 250 candidates, education analysts evaluate schools across four balanced indicators: Overall Mean Score (out of 12.00), University Transition Rate (% scoring C+ and above), Plain A / A- Concentration, and Year-over-Year (YoY) Value-Added Improvement.
Our interactive KCSE School Rankings directory aggregates historical KNEC performance benchmarks across National, Extra-County, County, and Private secondary schools across Kenya.

complianceTips: Under the CBC transition, former National, Extra-County, and County secondary schools are categorized as Senior Schools (Grades 10–12) offering specialized STEM, Social Science, and Arts & Sports pathways.
Always verify a school's registration status and boarding fee ceilings against official Ministry of Education guidelines.

faq.question: How are KCSE school rankings determined?
faq.answer: Rankings are based on each school's mean score — the average of all students' mean grades on a 12-point scale (A=12, E=1). This is calculated by KNEC (Kenya National Examinations Council).

faq.question: When are KCSE results released?
faq.answer: KCSE results are typically released by KNEC in March/April of the following year. The CS for Education announces the results and overall statistics.

faq.question: What is the difference between National, Extra-County, and County schools?
faq.answer: National schools admit students from all 47 counties. Extra-County schools admit from multiple counties but not all. County schools primarily serve their home county. Sub-County schools serve specific sub-counties.

faq.question: What mean score is needed for university admission?
faq.answer: The minimum KUCCPS university admission grade is typically C+ (mean score 7.0+). However, competitive courses like Medicine require A or A- (10.5+) and Engineering requires B+ (9.5+).

kra-car-import-calculator.notesTitle: KRA CRSP Motor Vehicle Import Duty, Age Depreciation & Port Clearing Guide (2026)
overview: Importing a motor vehicle into Kenya—whether from Japan, the United Kingdom, Dubai, Singapore, or South Africa—is governed by the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) Customs & Border Control Department and the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS). Instead of using your commercial invoice price (which could be under-declared), KRA calculates import taxes using the official Current Retail Selling Price (CRSP) database, which assigns a standardized showroom value for every vehicle make, model, engine capacity, and trim.

From the CRSP baseline, KRA deducts a statutory age depreciation allowance (up to 65% for vehicles 7 to 8 years old) to determine the Customs Value, and then applies a cumulative cascade of six statutory taxes and port levies: Import Duty (35%), Excise Duty (20%–35%), Value Added Tax (16%), Import Declaration Fee (IDF at 2.5%), Railway Development Levy (RDL at 2.0%), and NTSA registration fees.
howItWorks: Select a popular Kenyan import model from our CRSP preset list (e.g., Mazda Demio, Toyota Fielder, Subaru Forester, Toyota Harrier, Prado, or Hilux) or enter any custom CRSP showroom price.
Select the vehicle's age since first registration (up to the strict KEBS 8-year age limit), engine CC, and fuel type (Petrol, Diesel, Hybrid, or 100% Electric).
Inspect the exact cascading tax formula showing how Import Duty, Excise Value, 16% VAT, IDF, RDL, and NTSA logbook/plate charges build up your total Mombasa Port clearing cost.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Importing a 7-Year-Old 1,500cc Petrol Car (CRSP KES 2,950,000)
workedExample.scenario: Importing a 2019 Toyota Fielder / Mazda CX-3 (1,496cc Petrol, 7 years old) with an official KRA CRSP of KES 2,950,000:
steps: Age Depreciation (7 to ≤8 years = 65% discount): KES 2,950,000 × (1 − 0.65) = KES 1,032,500 Customs Value
1. Import Duty (35% of Customs Value): KES 361,375
2. Excise Value (Customs Value + Import Duty): KES 1,393,875 → Excise Duty (20% for ≤1500cc): KES 278,775
3. VAT Value (Excise Value + Excise Duty): KES 1,672,650 → VAT (16%): KES 267,624
4. IDF (2.5% of Customs Value): KES 25,813 + RDL (2.0% of Customs Value): KES 20,650
5. NTSA Registration & Number Plates (1,500cc): ~KES 13,550
Total KRA Taxes & Registration Payable: KES 967,787
workedExample.takeaway: Because Excise Duty is charged on (Customs Value + Import Duty) and VAT is charged on (Customs Value + Import Duty + Excise Duty), the effective cumulative tax rate on a standard petrol car is ~92% of its depreciated Customs Value.

complianceTips: KEBS 8-Year Rule (KS 1515:2000): Any vehicle whose year of first registration is more than 8 years prior to the year of importation is strictly prohibited and will be denied entry at Mombasa Port.

All used vehicles imported from Japan, UAE, UK, Singapore, Thailand, and South Africa must undergo mandatory Pre-Export Verification of Conformity (PVoC) inspection by QISJ (Quality Inspection Services Japan) before shipping.
Direct Imports of agricultural tractors, ambulances, and specialized prime movers enjoy 0% Import Duty exemptions under the EAC Common External Tariff.
notes: Select vehicle make, model, engine capacity, fuel type, and year of first registration to compute total Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) customs taxes using the official Current Retail Selling Price (CRSP) schedule.

See a complete statutory breakdown of age depreciation (up to 65% for vehicles 7–8 years old), Import Duty (35%), Excise Duty, 16% VAT, Import Declaration Fee (IDF 2.5%), and Railway Development Levy (RDL 2%).
Verify KEBS 8-year age limit compliance and NTSA registration fees before shipping a vehicle to the Port of Mombasa.

faq.question: Why does the year of manufacture matter so much for car imports in Kenya?
faq.answer: KRA applies progressive depreciation up to 65% on a vehicle's Current Retail Selling Price (CRSP) based on age, and KEBS prohibits the importation of vehicles older than 8 years from the year of first registration.

faq.question: Are all KRA port taxes stacked on top of each other?
faq.answer: Yes. Excise Duty applies on (Customs Value + Import Duty), and 16% VAT applies on (Customs Value + Import Duty + Excise Duty), plus IDF (2.5%) and RDL (2.0%).

faq.question: How does the KEBS 8-year age limit rule work when importing a car to Kenya in 2026?
faq.answer: Under KS 1515:2000 enforced by the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) and NTSA, a used motor vehicle imported into Kenya must be Less than 8 years old from its year of first registration. In 2026, only vehicles first registered in 2019 or later (with a pre-export Roadworthiness Inspection Certificate from QISJ) are allowed entry at the Port of Mombasa.

faq.question: Why does KRA use the CRSP schedule instead of my Japanese auction invoice price?
faq.answer: Under the East African Community Customs Management Act (EACCMA), KRA values used motor vehicles using the standardized Current Retail Selling Price (CRSP) database—representing the new showroom price of that exact make, model, and engine capacity—and applies a fixed statutory age depreciation schedule (up to 65% for vehicles 7–8 years old) to prevent invoice under-valuation.

faq.question: In what order are KRA car import taxes cascaded at Mombasa Port?
faq.answer: First, KRA deducts age depreciation and 25.5% showroom markup from the CRSP to get the Customs Value (CV). Second, Import Duty (35%) is charged on CV. Third, Excise Duty (20%–35%) is charged on (CV + Import Duty). Fourth, VAT (16%) is charged on (CV + Import Duty + Excise Duty). Finally, Import Declaration Fee (IDF at 2.5% of CV) and Railway Development Levy (RDL at 2% of CV) are added.

number-plate-decoder.notesTitle: NTSA Vehicle Registration Series (KAA–KDU) & Special Plates Guide
overview: Every motor vehicle, trailer, motorcycle, and three-wheeler operating on Kenyan public roads must be registered with the National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) under the Traffic Act (Cap 403). Since 1989, Kenya has used the second-generation 3-letter series starting from KAA 001A up to the current KDU/KDV blocks, omitting the letters I and O to prevent ambiguity with numerals 1 and 0.

Knowing the registration year corresponding to a 3-letter prefix (e.g., KBA = 2007, KCA = 2014, KDA = 2020, KDU = 2025/2026) is essential when buying a used car in Kenya to verify whether the vehicle was imported at the maximum 7-year age limit or registered brand-new locally.
howItWorks: Type any Kenyan registration plate (such as KDU 450A, KDA 210M, GK B412, 47 CG 001A, or 29 CD 1K) into the decoder input.
The tool parses civilian K-series prefixes, diplomatic CD/CC codes, national government GK prefixes, county government CG codes, and motorcycle KM series.
Browse the complete chronological KAA-to-KDU timeline table and color-code reference below the decoder.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Verifying a Used Car's Import Year vs. Manufacture Year
workedExample.scenario: A seller advertises a '2018 Toyota Harrier' bearing number plate KDA 412J:
steps: Decoding Prefix KDA: Issued by NTSA between July and September 2020.
Implication: If the car was registered as KDA in 2020, it was most likely manufactured in 2013 (imported at 7 years old in 2020)—unless it was imported nearly brand-new in 2020!
Verification: Perform an official NTSA TIMS online motor vehicle copy-of-records search (KES 550 on eCitizen) to confirm the exact Year of Manufacture and registered owner.
workedExample.takeaway: In Kenya, a car's number plate prefix shows the Year of Kenyan Registration, which is usually 7 years later than the Year of Manufacture for used Japanese imports.

complianceTips: Always run a KES 550 NTSA TIMS vehicle search on eCitizen before paying a deposit on any used vehicle to verify that there are no bank chattel mortgages or caveats.
Ensure the vehicle is fitted with the new reflective NTSA smart number plates featuring the Kenyan coat of arms, laser hologram, and QR serial code.
notes: Enter any Kenyan vehicle registration prefix (e.g., KDA, KDM, KBZ, GK, CD, KX, ZB) to decode its approximate year of registration, historical county code, or special diplomatic/government series.
Browse the chronological K-series registration timeline from legacy colonial/provincial prefixes (KA–KZ) through second-generation (KAA–KAZ) and third-generation (KBA–KDZ) NTSA series.
Reference data is compiled from National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) motor vehicle registration records.

faq.question: What do Kenya number plate prefixes mean?
faq.answer: Kenya plates follow the format KXX 000X (3-letter prefix, 3 digits, 1 letter). The prefix historically indicated the county of registration and approximate year. Since most registrations now happen centrally in Nairobi, newer prefixes mainly indicate the year of registration.

faq.question: What does GK mean on a Kenya plate?
faq.answer: GK stands for 'Government of Kenya' and is used on all central government vehicles. These plates are white with blue text.

faq.question: What is a CD number plate in Kenya?
faq.answer: CD plates belong to diplomatic corps (foreign embassies and consulates). The number after CD indicates the country. CC plates are for consular corps.

faq.question: Why are letters I and O missing from Kenya plates?
faq.answer: The letters I and O are omitted from Kenya registration plate prefixes to avoid confusion with the numbers 1 and 0.

faq.question: Can I get a personalized number plate in Kenya?
faq.answer: Yes, NTSA offers personalized/vanity plates for an additional fee. However, these plates cannot be decoded to determine registration county or year.

driving-license-guide.notesTitle: NTSA Smart Driving License Classes (A–G), TIMS Fees & Endorsement Guide
overview: Under the Traffic Act (Cap 403) and NTSA Smart Driving License regulations, Kenya categorizes motor vehicle drivers into seven harmonized classes (Classes A through G) aligned with East African Community (EAC) standards. Every driver must transition from a Provisional Driving License (PDL) through an accredited driving school, pass the NTSA theory and practical yard/road test, and obtain a biometric chip-embedded Smart Driving License via the eCitizen TIMS portal.

Commercial truck drivers (Class C), public service matatu/bus drivers (Class D), and commercial motorcycle couriers (Class A2/A3) must meet strict age and experience progression intervals before endorsing higher classes.
howItWorks: Switch between the License Classes (A–G), Application Process, and Official NTSA Fee Schedule tabs.
Check the minimum statutory age, maximum vehicle weight/passenger capacity, and prerequisite years of driving experience required for each class.
Follow the 6-step eCitizen TIMS workflow for PDL issuance, test booking, biometric capture, and 1-year vs. 3-year Smart DL renewal.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Total Statutory Cost to Obtain a Class B (Light Vehicle) Smart DL
workedExample.scenario: A first-time learner driver applying for a Class B1/B2 (Automatic or Manual Saloon/SUV) driving license via eCitizen:
steps: 1. Provisional Driving License (PDL — valid 3 months): KES 650
2. Driving Test Booking Fee (NTSA Theory & Practical Examination): KES 1,050
3. Biometric Smart Driving License (3-Year Validity): KES 3,050
Total Official NTSA / eCitizen Statutory Fees: KES 4,750 (excluding driving school tuition of KES 12,000–18,000)
workedExample.takeaway: Choosing a 3-year Smart DL renewal (KES 3,050) instead of three separate 1-year renewals saves time and repeated eCitizen convenience fees.

complianceTips: To qualify for a Class D1/D2 PSV endorsement (Matatu or Bus), a driver must be at least 22 years old, hold a Class B license for at least 3–4 years, and hold a valid NTSA PSV Badge.
Driving with an expired license or operating a vehicle class not endorsed on your Smart DL attracts an instant NTSA fine of KES 3,000 to KES 10,000.
notes: Select a driving license category (Class A motorcycles, Class B light vehicles, Class C commercial trucks, Class D PSVs, or Class G industrial equipment) to view NTSA age, endorsement, and upgrade rules.
Review step-by-step eCitizen TIMS application procedures from Provisional Driving License (PDL) enrollment through theory/practical testing to Smart Driving License collection.
Fee schedules reflect published National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) citizen service rates.

faq.question: How do I get a driving license in Kenya?
faq.answer: The process involves: 1. Getting a medical check (DL Form 1), 2. Enrolling in an NTSA-approved driving school, 3. Getting a provisional license (PDL), 4. Passing a theory test, 5. Passing a practical driving test, and finally 6. Paying for and collecting your license.

faq.question: What is the age limit for a driving license in Kenya?
faq.answer: You must be at least 18 years old for Class A (motorcycles), Class B (cars), and Class G (tractors). For Class C (heavy vehicles) you must be 21, for Class BCE (trailers) you must be 24, and for driving instructors you must be 25.

faq.question: How much does a driving license cost in Kenya?
faq.answer: The NTSA Smart Driving Licence fee is KES 3,050 and it is valid for 3 years. The total cost including driving school fees, medical checks, provisional licenses, and test fees varies by class and provider; confirm the payable amount in eCitizen.

faq.question: How long is a Kenyan driving license valid?
faq.answer: The NTSA Smart Driving Licence is valid for 3 years from the date of issue. The current renewal fee is KES 3,050; confirm the amount in eCitizen before payment.

faq.question: Do I need a new Smart Driving License?
faq.answer: Yes, NTSA is phasing out the old red booklet licenses. All new applications and renewals are issued as the new digital Smart Driving License card, which contains a microchip with your driver profile and demerit points.

traffic-fines.notesTitle: Kenya Traffic Act (Cap 403) Offences, Minor Fines & Demerit Points Guide
overview: Road traffic enforcement in Kenya is governed by the Traffic Act (Cap 403), the NTSA (Operation of Public Service Vehicles) Regulations, and the scheduled Minor Traffic Offences statutory notice. Under Kenyan law, scheduled minor traffic offences carry fixed statutory fines (ranging from KES 500 to KES 10,000) payable exclusively through official government digital channels or court cash bail, while serious offences (such as drunk driving, causing death by dangerous driving, or operating an unroadworthy vehicle) require mandatory court appearance.
Knowing the exact statutory fine for each offence protects motorists, boda boda riders, and PSV crews from roadside extortion and unlawful vehicle impoundment.
howItWorks: Filter traffic offences by category (Speeding, Licensing, Seatbelts & Safety, PSV/Matatu Rules, Motorcycle/Boda Boda, Obstruction, or Serious Offences) or search by keyword.
Check the exact Traffic Act section, statutory fine range (KES), and NTSA Smart DL demerit points attached to each violation.
Review the legal rights of motorists at police roadblocks and official eCitizen/Court payment procedures.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Speeding Offence Thresholds Under Section 42 of the Traffic Act
workedExample.scenario: A motorist is flagged at a speed check along the Nairobi–Nakuru Highway in a 100 km/h zone:
steps: Exceeding speed limit by 1 to 5 km/h: Statutory warning or KES 500 fine
Exceeding speed limit by 6 to 10 km/h: KES 3,000 fine
Exceeding speed limit by 11 to 15 km/h: KES 6,000 fine
Exceeding speed limit by 16 to 20 km/h: KES 10,000 fine (or court prosecution)
workedExample.takeaway: PSV matatus, buses, and commercial trucks are legally speed-governed at 80 km/h in Kenya—tampering with a speed governor carries heavy fines and immediate suspension of the vehicle's TLB/NTSA inspection sticker.

complianceTips: Never pay cash bribes at a police check—all legitimate traffic fines are paid via the Judiciary e-Filing / KCB court cash bail PayBill or eCitizen NTSA portal with an official receipt.
Accumulating 12 or more demerit points on your Smart Driving License within 24 months triggers mandatory license suspension under NTSA regulations.
notes: Search or filter traffic offences under the Traffic Act (Cap 403) and NTSA Minor Offences Rules—covering speeding, PSV compliance, driving without valid insurance or license, and vehicle roadworthiness.
Inspect statutory cash bail/fine ceilings (KES), court penalties, and driver demerit point assessments.
Minor traffic fines are payable strictly through official eCitizen / NTSA digital channels or designated court registries—never pay unreceipted cash bribes on the road.

faq.question: What is the fine for speeding in Kenya?
faq.answer: Speeding fines range from KES 5,000 for exceeding the limit by up to 10 km/h, to KES 50,000 for exceeding by over 40 km/h. Higher speed offences also carry more demerit points and may result in arrest.

faq.question: What is the NTSA demerit points system?
faq.answer: Kenya uses a 24-point demerit system over a 3-year period. Points 1–12 result in a warning, 13–18 require a mandatory road safety course, 19–23 lead to license suspension for 6 months, and 24+ points result in license revocation.

faq.question: What is the fine for driving without insurance in Kenya?
faq.answer: Driving without valid motor vehicle insurance carries a fine of up to KES 50,000 and is an arrestable offence. You can also face imprisonment. Insurance is a legal requirement under Cap 405.

faq.question: How do I pay NTSA traffic fines?
faq.answer: You can pay via: cash bond at the police station, M-Pesa paybill (NTSA service), eCitizen portal (ntsa.go.ke), or through court-imposed fine after a hearing.

faq.question: What is the fine for drunk driving in Kenya?
faq.answer: First offence DUI carries a fine of KES 100,000 plus license suspension for 1 year or imprisonment up to 2 years. Repeat offenders face KES 200,000 fine plus license revocation and up to 3 years imprisonment.

national-parks-directory.notesTitle: Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) 2026 Park Entry Fees & Safari Planning Guide

Entry tariffs are structured into three residency tiers—East African Citizens (KES), Kenyan Residents (KES), and Non-Residents (USD)—and by park classification (Premium Parks, Wilderness Parks, Urban/Scenic Parks, and Marine Parks).

faq.question: How much does it cost to enter a national park in Kenya?
faq.answer: Entry fees vary by park and visitor category. Kenyan citizens pay KES 200–500/day, residents KES 400–2,500/day, and non-residents USD 15–90/day. Children pay approximately half. Premium parks like Maasai Mara and Amboseli charge more.

faq.question: What is the difference between a national park and a national reserve?
faq.answer: National parks are managed by Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) with no human settlement or grazing allowed. National reserves are managed by county governments and may allow some pastoral activities.

faq.question: What is the Big Five?
faq.answer: The Big Five are: Lion, Leopard, Elephant, Rhinoceros, and Cape Buffalo. The best parks to see all five include Maasai Mara, Lake Nakuru, and Ol Pejeta Conservancy.

faq.question: When is the best time for safari in Kenya?
faq.answer: The dry season (June–October) is best for wildlife viewing as animals gather around water sources. The Great Wildebeest Migration crosses into Maasai Mara from July–October. However, the green season (November–May) offers lower rates and fewer crowds.

faq.question: How do I book a KWS park visit?
faq.answer: You can book through the eCitizen portal (ecitizen.go.ke) or pay at the gate. For popular parks, advance booking is recommended, especially during peak season (July–October and December–January).

Planting maize, beans, potatoes, sorghum, or horticultural crops even two weeks after the onset of effective rains can reduce grain yields by 15% to 30% due to missed nitrogen mineralization (the 'Birch effect') and terminal moisture stress during flowering.

faq.question: When should I plant maize in Kenya?
faq.answer: For the Long Rains season, plant maize in March–April in most regions. For Short Rains, plant in October (Nyanza, Coast, Eastern). Highland areas like the Rift Valley typically only have one season.

faq.question: What is intercropping and why is it recommended?
faq.answer: Intercropping means growing two or more crops together in the same field. The classic Kenyan example is maize + beans. Benefits include better soil fertility (legumes fix nitrogen), reduced pest pressure, and diversified income.

faq.question: Where can I get certified seeds in Kenya?
faq.answer: Buy from KEPHIS-registered seed dealers, Kenya Seed Company outlets, or licensed agrovets. Always check the KEPHIS certification label on the packet for germination guarantee.

faq.question: What are Kenya's two farming seasons?
faq.answer: Kenya has two main seasons: the 'Long Rains' (March–May) and 'Short Rains' (October–December). However, highland and western regions may have slightly different timing, and some areas only support one season.

faq.question: How do I know which crops suit my area?
faq.answer: Consider your altitude, annual rainfall, and soil type. Contact your local KALRO research station or county agricultural extension officer for personalized advice.

faq.question: How do I register for subsidized fertilizer in Kenya?

faq.question: How much cheaper is subsidized fertilizer?
faq.answer: Subsidized DAP costs approximately KES 2,500 per 50kg bag vs KES 5,500+ at market prices — a saving of over 50%. CAN is KES 1,800 subsidized vs KES 4,000 at market price.

faq.question: Which fertilizer should I use for maize?
faq.answer: Use DAP or NPK 23-23-0 at planting (for phosphorus and root development), then top-dress with CAN or Urea when the maize is knee-high (for nitrogen and vegetative growth).

faq.question: What affects livestock prices in Kenya?
faq.answer: Prices vary by animal condition/weight, breed, season (prices spike before Eid, Christmas, Easter), drought conditions (supply increase = lower prices), and market location.

faq.question: Where is the biggest livestock market in Kenya?
faq.answer: Dagoretti Market in Nairobi is the largest urban livestock market. For pastoral areas, Garissa and Isiolo are major trading hubs.

faq.question: How do I sell livestock at a market?
faq.answer: Bring your animals to the market on designated market days. You'll need a livestock movement permit from your local veterinary officer. Buyers negotiate directly with sellers.

faq.question: Are residential houses exempt from the NCA construction levy?
faq.answer: Projects receive county architectural/structural plan approvals and NCA registration; always use an NCA-registered contractor and licensed structural engineer.

faq.question: How many machine-cut stones (9×9×18 inches) are needed per square metre of wall in Kenya?
faq.answer: Standard Kenyan 200mm (9-inch) machine-cut quarry stones from Ndarugo, Juja, or Naivasha measure 225mm × 225mm × 450mm. Accounting for a 15mm mortar bed and 5% cutting/breakage wastage, 1 square metre of wall requires approximately 11 stones.

faq.question: What approvals are required before starting residential house construction (Mjengo) in Kenya?
faq.answer: For formal residential construction in Kenya, you require County Government architectural and structural plan approvals (signed by a BORAQS-registered architect and EBK structural engineer), a NEMA Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) license for multi-unit or commercial projects, and project registration with the National Construction Authority (NCA).

faq.question: Why do construction costs per square metre vary across Nairobi, Mombasa, and Western Kenya?

overview: Protecting your brand name, logo, software, invention, or creative work in Kenya is governed by two primary state agencies: the Kenya Industrial Property Institute (KIPI) under the Trade Marks Act (Cap 506) and Industrial Property Act (2001) for Trademarks, Patents, Utility Models, and Industrial Designs, and the Kenya Copyright Board (KECOBO) under the Copyright Act (Cap 130) for literary, musical, artistic, audio-visual, and software works.

Registering a trademark with KIPI grants you 10 years of renewable exclusive statutory rights across Kenya under the International Nice Classification (Classes 1–34 for Goods and Classes 35–45 for Services), enabling you to block counterfeits via the Anti-Counterfeit Authority (ACA).
howItWorks: Select the Intellectual Property right you wish to register: Trademark (KIPI), Patent (KIPI), Utility Model, Industrial Design, or Copyright (KECOBO).

For Trademarks, specify the number of Nice Classification classes (1 to 45) to compute the exact statutory fees across Preliminary Search (TM 27), Application Filing (TM 2), KIPI Journal Advertisement, and Registration Certificate (TM 11).
Compare official statutory government fees for Kenyan citizens/SMEs across each stage of the registration lifecycle.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Registering a Brand Logo in 1 Nice Class at KIPI (Kenyan Applicant)
workedExample.scenario: A Kenyan startup registers its brand name and logo in Class 35 (Retail & Business Services) directly at KIPI:
steps: Stage 1 — Preliminary Availability Search (Form TM 27, optional but recommended): KES 3,000
Stage 2 — Application to Register a Trademark in 1st Class (Form TM 2): KES 4,000
Stage 3 — Advertisement in the KIPI Industrial Property Journal (60-day opposition window): KES 3,000
Stage 4 — Issuance of Certificate of Registration (Form TM 11, valid 10 years): KES 2,000
Total Statutory KIPI Government Fees (1 Class): KES 12,000 (KES 9,000 if skipping TM 27 search)
workedExample.takeaway: Each additional Nice Class filed within the same trademark application costs slightly less than a standalone first-class filing—always cover both your product class and your retail/service class.

complianceTips: Once a trademark is examined and approved, it must be advertised in the monthly KIPI Journal for 60 days to allow third-party opposition before the final certificate is issued.
Software code, mobile apps, books, and music are registered online via the KECOBO National Rights Registry (NRR) portal on eCitizen for KES 1,000 per work.
notes: Select applicant residency status (Kenyan Citizen/Local Entity vs. Foreign Applicant) and number of Nice Classification classes (1 to 45) to calculate official Kenya Industrial Property Institute (KIPI) trademark registration fees.

Review stage-by-stage statutory fees from preliminary TM27 search and TM2 application filing through Industrial Property Journal advertisement (60-day opposition window) to 10-year registration certificate issuance.
Fee schedules reflect the Industrial Property Act and gazetted KIPI tariff regulations.

faq.question: How much does it cost to register a trademark in Kenya?
faq.answer: The total KIPI fees for registering a trademark in one class are approximately KES 22,450. This includes search (KES 1,000), application (KES 3,850), examination (KES 5,500), Gazette publication (KES 3,300), registration (KES 7,700), and certificate (KES 1,100). Attorney fees are separate.

faq.question: How long does trademark registration take in Kenya?
faq.answer: Trademark registration typically takes 12–18 months from application to certificate issuance. This includes the 60-day opposition period after Gazette publication.

faq.question: What are trademark classes?
faq.answer: The Nice Classification divides goods and services into 45 classes (34 goods, 11 services). You need to register in each class relevant to your business. Each additional class costs KES 3,080 on top of the base application fee.

faq.question: What is the difference between a patent and a utility model?
faq.answer: A patent protects novel inventions for 20 years and requires thorough examination (costs ~KES 34,650). A utility model (petty patent) is simpler, faster (6–12 months), cheaper (~KES 13,750), but only lasts 10 years and has a lower inventiveness threshold.

faq.question: Do I need an IP attorney?
faq.answer: While not strictly required for Kenyan nationals, using a registered IP agent/attorney is highly recommended. They handle the technical filing process and respond to KIPI queries. Foreign applicants must use a registered Kenyan IP agent.

professional-bodies-kenya.notesTitle: Kenya Statutory Professional Regulatory Boards & License Verification Guide
overview: In Kenya, practicing a regulated profession—such as medicine, law, engineering, accounting, architecture, quantity surveying, pharmacy, nursing, teaching, or real estate agency—without a valid current practicing certificate from the relevant statutory board is a criminal offence under the respective Act of Parliament.

Our directory consolidates 24 statutory professional regulatory councils and boards in Kenya, providing their enabling legislation, initial registration fees, annual practicing renewal fees, academic admission requirements, and direct links to their public practitioner verification portals.
howItWorks: Search by profession (e.g., Doctor, Advocate, Engineer, CPA Accountant, Architect, Contractor, Pharmacist, Teacher), board name, or acronym (KMPDC, LSK, EBK, ICPAK, BORAQS, NCA, TSC, PPB).
Inspect initial registration fees, annual practicing license renewal costs, and mandatory CPD (Continuing Professional Development) requirements.
Click the official verification portal link to confirm whether a practitioner is in good standing for the current calendar year.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: How to Verify a Doctor, Lawyer, Engineer, or Architect Before Hiring
workedExample.scenario: Protecting yourself or your business from unqualified quacks before signing a contract or undergoing treatment:
steps: Medical Doctors & Clinics: Check the KMPDC Master Register at kmpdc.go.ke or send an SMS with the doctor's name/registration number to 20547.
Advocates / Lawyers: Search the Law Society of Kenya (LSK) Advocate Search Portal at online.lsk.or.ke to confirm an active 2026 Practicing Certificate.
Professional Engineers: Check the Engineers Board of Kenya (EBK) register at ebk.go.ke (Graduate Engineers cannot stamp structural drawings—only Registered Professional/Consulting Engineers can).
Architects & Quantity Surveyors: Verify active registration on the BORAQS portal (boraqs.or.ke).
workedExample.takeaway: Holding a university degree alone does not authorize a professional to practice independently in Kenya—they must hold a current annual Practicing Certificate from their statutory board.

complianceTips: Most Kenyan professional boards run a January 1 to December 31 practicing year and require 20 to 40 Continuing Professional Development (CPD) points annually prior to renewal.
Always ask for a practitioner's registration number and cross-check it on the official board portal before paying professional retainers.
notes: Search Kenya's statutory professional regulatory bodies and licensing councils by profession, acronym (LSK, KMPDC, EBK, ICPAK, BORAQS, NCK, PPB, TSC, EARB), or enabling Act of Parliament.
Compare initial registration fees, annual practicing certificate renewal costs, academic qualification requirements, and direct links to official online practitioner verification registers.
Always verify a practitioner's current annual license status on the regulator's portal before engaging professional legal, medical, engineering, or financial services.

faq.question: How do I verify if a professional is registered in Kenya?
faq.answer: Each regulatory body has a public register or verification portal. Use the verification URL provided for each body in our directory. For doctors, check kmpdc.go.ke; for lawyers, check lsk.or.ke/find-a-lawyer.

faq.question: Is professional registration mandatory in Kenya?
faq.answer: Yes, practising a regulated profession without valid registration is a criminal offence under the respective Acts. This applies to doctors, lawyers, engineers, accountants, nurses, and many other professions.

faq.question: How much does professional registration cost?
faq.answer: Costs vary widely — from KES 1,000 (TSC for teachers) to KES 20,000+ (CMA for investment advisors). Most bodies charge KES 3,000–10,000 for initial registration plus annual renewal fees.

passport-id-fees.notesTitle: Kenya e-Passport (34/50/66-Page), Maisha Namba ID & Civil Registration Guide (2026)
overview: Applications for Kenyan East African Community (EAC) biometric e-Passports, National Identity Cards (Maisha Namba), Birth Certificates, and Death Certificates are processed digitally through the eCitizen portal by the Directorate of Immigration Services and the Civil Registration Services (CRS) under the Ministry of Interior and National Administration.

Following the 2024/2026 gazetted fee revisions, knowing the exact page count tariff (A-Series 34-page, B-Series 50-page, or C-Series 66-page), replacement penalties for lost/mutilated passports, and required supporting documents prevents application rejections at Nyayo House or regional immigration offices.
howItWorks: Compare official 2026 gazetted fees across 34-page, 50-page, and 66-page Kenyan e-Passports, Diplomatic Passports, Lost/Mutilated replacements, National IDs, and Civil Registration certificates.
Review the mandatory document checklist (original ID, birth certificate, parents' IDs, recommender details, and old passport for renewals).
Locate the 8 regional Directorate of Immigration biometric capture stations (Nairobi Nyayo House, Mombasa, Kisumu, Nakuru, Eldoret, Embu, Kisii, and Kericho) plus diaspora embassies.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Choosing Between a 34-Page (A-Series) and 50-Page (B-Series) e-Passport
workedExample.scenario: An applicant on eCitizen comparing the 10-year cost of an A-Series vs. B-Series Kenyan e-Passport:
steps: 34-Page Ordinary e-Passport (A-Series, valid 10 years): KES 7,500
50-Page Ordinary e-Passport (B-Series, valid 10 years): KES 9,500 (only KES 2,000 extra for 16 additional visa pages)
66-Page Frequent Traveller e-Passport (C-Series, valid 10 years): KES 12,500
Lost Passport Replacement Fee: KES 20,000 (requires a Police Abstract and sworn Affidavit) · Mutilated Passport Replacement: KES 10,000
workedExample.takeaway: Because Kenyan e-Passports cannot have extra pages stitched in once full, frequent regional or international travellers save money by selecting the 50-page (KES 9,500) or 66-page (KES 12,500) booklet upfront.

complianceTips: All passport applications and fee payments are completed strictly online via ecitizen.go.ke—never pay middlemen or brokers outside Nyayo House.
First-time National ID registration for Kenyan youths turning 18 is KES 300 (or free during gazetted registration drives), while replacing a lost ID costs KES 1,000.
notes: Filter official Directorate of Immigration and Citizen Services fees by document category: e-Passports (34-page A Series, 50-page B Series, 66-page C Series), Maisha Namba / National ID cards, Civil Registration (Birth & Death Certificates), and Foreign National permits.
Review required supporting documents, biometric booking procedures on eCitizen, and standard processing timelines at Nyayo House and regional Huduma Centres.
All statutory payments must be completed exclusively through the official eCitizen gateway (ecitizen.go.ke).

faq.question: How much is a new passport in Kenya?
faq.answer: Passport fees vary by passport type and the current Immigration fee schedule. See the fee table above and confirm the amount shown in eCitizen before payment.

faq.question: How long does it take to get a Kenyan passport?
faq.answer: The official processing time is 10–15 working days after biometric capture. However, wait times can sometimes be longer depending on backlog. An expedited/emergency passport takes 1–3 days.

faq.question: How much does it cost to replace a lost National ID?
faq.answer: Replacement of a lost or damaged National ID is currently free under the government fee waiver. A lost ID still requires a police abstract, while a damaged ID should be surrendered. Confirm the waiver is still active before applying.

faq.question: How do I apply for a passport in Kenya?
faq.answer: The entire process starts online via the eCitizen portal. You fill out the application, pay the fees, and book an appointment. Then you visit the Immigration office or Huduma Centre on your appointment date with original documents for biometrics.
