Compare school mean points and university transition trends to support informed Senior School selection.
Data is compiled from published post-examination academic performance disclosures and Ministry of Education school classifications.

faq.question: How are KCSE school rankings determined?
faq.answer: Rankings are based on each school's mean score — the average of all students' mean grades on a 12-point scale (A=12, E=1). This is calculated by KNEC (Kenya National Examinations Council).

faq.question: When are KCSE results released?
faq.answer: KCSE results are typically released by KNEC in March/April of the following year. The CS for Education announces the results and overall statistics.

faq.question: What is the difference between National, Extra-County, and County schools?
faq.answer: National schools admit students from all 47 counties. Extra-County schools admit from multiple counties but not all. County schools primarily serve their home county. Sub-County schools serve specific sub-counties.

faq.question: What mean score is needed for university admission?
faq.answer: The minimum KUCCPS university admission grade is typically C+ (mean score 7.0+). However, competitive courses like Medicine require A or A- (10.5+) and Engineering requires B+ (9.5+).

kra-car-import-calculator.notesTitle: KRA CRSP Motor Vehicle Import Duty, Age Depreciation & Port Clearing Guide (2026)
overview: Importing a motor vehicle into Kenya—whether from Japan, the United Kingdom, Dubai, Singapore, or South Africa—is governed by the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) Customs & Border Control Department and the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS). Instead of using your commercial invoice price (which could be under-declared), KRA calculates import taxes using the official Current Retail Selling Price (CRSP) database, which assigns a standardized showroom value for every vehicle make, model, engine capacity, and trim.

From the CRSP baseline, KRA deducts a statutory age depreciation allowance (up to 65% for vehicles 7 to 8 years old) to determine the Customs Value, and then applies a cumulative cascade of six statutory taxes and port levies: Import Duty (35%), Excise Duty (20%–35%), Value Added Tax (16%), Import Declaration Fee (IDF at 2.5%), Railway Development Levy (RDL at 2.0%), and NTSA registration fees.
howItWorks: Select a popular Kenyan import model from our CRSP preset list (e.g., Mazda Demio, Toyota Fielder, Subaru Forester, Toyota Harrier, Prado, or Hilux) or enter any custom CRSP showroom price.
Select the vehicle's age since first registration (up to the strict KEBS 8-year age limit), engine CC, and fuel type (Petrol, Diesel, Hybrid, or 100% Electric).
Inspect the exact cascading tax formula showing how Import Duty, Excise Value, 16% VAT, IDF, RDL, and NTSA logbook/plate charges build up your total Mombasa Port clearing cost.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Importing a 7-Year-Old 1,500cc Petrol Car (CRSP KES 2,950,000)
workedExample.scenario: Importing a 2019 Toyota Fielder / Mazda CX-3 (1,496cc Petrol, 7 years old) with an official KRA CRSP of KES 2,950,000:
steps: Age Depreciation (7 to ≤8 years = 65% discount): KES 2,950,000 × (1 − 0.65) = KES 1,032,500 Customs Value
1. Import Duty (35% of Customs Value): KES 361,375
2. Excise Value (Customs Value + Import Duty): KES 1,393,875 → Excise Duty (20% for ≤1500cc): KES 278,775
3. VAT Value (Excise Value + Excise Duty): KES 1,672,650 → VAT (16%): KES 267,624
4. IDF (2.5% of Customs Value): KES 25,813 + RDL (2.0% of Customs Value): KES 20,650
5. NTSA Registration & Number Plates (1,500cc): ~KES 13,550
Total KRA Taxes & Registration Payable: KES 967,787
workedExample.takeaway: Because Excise Duty is charged on (Customs Value + Import Duty) and VAT is charged on (Customs Value + Import Duty + Excise Duty), the effective cumulative tax rate on a standard petrol car is ~92% of its depreciated Customs Value.

complianceTips: KEBS 8-Year Rule (KS 1515:2000): Any vehicle whose year of first registration is more than 8 years prior to the year of importation is strictly prohibited and will be denied entry at Mombasa Port.

All used vehicles imported from Japan, UAE, UK, Singapore, Thailand, and South Africa must undergo mandatory Pre-Export Verification of Conformity (PVoC) inspection by QISJ (Quality Inspection Services Japan) before shipping.
Direct Imports of agricultural tractors, ambulances, and specialized prime movers enjoy 0% Import Duty exemptions under the EAC Common External Tariff.
notes: Select vehicle make, model, engine capacity, fuel type, and year of first registration to compute total Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) customs taxes using the official Current Retail Selling Price (CRSP) schedule.

See a complete statutory breakdown of age depreciation (up to 65% for vehicles 7–8 years old), Import Duty (35%), Excise Duty, 16% VAT, Import Declaration Fee (IDF 2.5%), and Railway Development Levy (RDL 2%).
Verify KEBS 8-year age limit compliance and NTSA registration fees before shipping a vehicle to the Port of Mombasa.

faq.question: Why does the year of manufacture matter so much for car imports in Kenya?
faq.answer: KRA applies progressive depreciation up to 65% on a vehicle's Current Retail Selling Price (CRSP) based on age, and KEBS prohibits the importation of vehicles older than 8 years from the year of first registration.

faq.question: Are all KRA port taxes stacked on top of each other?
faq.answer: Yes. Excise Duty applies on (Customs Value + Import Duty), and 16% VAT applies on (Customs Value + Import Duty + Excise Duty), plus IDF (2.5%) and RDL (2.0%).

number-plate-decoder.notesTitle: NTSA Vehicle Registration Series (KAA–KDU) & Special Plates Guide
overview: Every motor vehicle, trailer, motorcycle, and three-wheeler operating on Kenyan public roads must be registered with the National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) under the Traffic Act (Cap 403). Since 1989, Kenya has used the second-generation 3-letter series starting from KAA 001A up to the current KDU/KDV blocks, omitting the letters I and O to prevent ambiguity with numerals 1 and 0.

Knowing the registration year corresponding to a 3-letter prefix (e.g., KBA = 2007, KCA = 2014, KDA = 2020, KDU = 2025/2026) is essential when buying a used car in Kenya to verify whether the vehicle was imported at the maximum 7-year age limit or registered brand-new locally.
howItWorks: Type any Kenyan registration plate (such as KDU 450A, KDA 210M, GK B412, 47 CG 001A, or 29 CD 1K) into the decoder input.
The tool parses civilian K-series prefixes, diplomatic CD/CC codes, national government GK prefixes, county government CG codes, and motorcycle KM series.
Browse the complete chronological KAA-to-KDU timeline table and color-code reference below the decoder.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Verifying a Used Car's Import Year vs. Manufacture Year
workedExample.scenario: A seller advertises a '2018 Toyota Harrier' bearing number plate KDA 412J:
steps: Decoding Prefix KDA: Issued by NTSA between July and September 2020.
Implication: If the car was registered as KDA in 2020, it was most likely manufactured in 2013 (imported at 7 years old in 2020)—unless it was imported nearly brand-new in 2020!
Verification: Perform an official NTSA TIMS online motor vehicle copy-of-records search (KES 550 on eCitizen) to confirm the exact Year of Manufacture and registered owner.
workedExample.takeaway: In Kenya, a car's number plate prefix shows the Year of Kenyan Registration, which is usually 7 years later than the Year of Manufacture for used Japanese imports.

complianceTips: Always run a KES 550 NTSA TIMS vehicle search on eCitizen before paying a deposit on any used vehicle to verify that there are no bank chattel mortgages or caveats.
Ensure the vehicle is fitted with the new reflective NTSA smart number plates featuring the Kenyan coat of arms, laser hologram, and QR serial code.
notes: Enter any Kenyan vehicle registration prefix (e.g., KDA, KDM, KBZ, GK, CD, KX, ZB) to decode its approximate year of registration, historical county code, or special diplomatic/government series.
Browse the chronological K-series registration timeline from legacy colonial/provincial prefixes (KA–KZ) through second-generation (KAA–KAZ) and third-generation (KBA–KDZ) NTSA series.
Reference data is compiled from National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) motor vehicle registration records.

faq.question: What do Kenya number plate prefixes mean?
faq.answer: Kenya plates follow the format KXX 000X (3-letter prefix, 3 digits, 1 letter). The prefix historically indicated the county of registration and approximate year. Since most registrations now happen centrally in Nairobi, newer prefixes mainly indicate the year of registration.

faq.question: What does GK mean on a Kenya plate?
faq.answer: GK stands for 'Government of Kenya' and is used on all central government vehicles. These plates are white with blue text.

faq.question: What is a CD number plate in Kenya?
faq.answer: CD plates belong to diplomatic corps (foreign embassies and consulates). The number after CD indicates the country. CC plates are for consular corps.

faq.question: Why are letters I and O missing from Kenya plates?
faq.answer: The letters I and O are omitted from Kenya registration plate prefixes to avoid confusion with the numbers 1 and 0.

faq.question: Can I get a personalized number plate in Kenya?
faq.answer: Yes, NTSA offers personalized/vanity plates for an additional fee. However, these plates cannot be decoded to determine registration county or year.

driving-license-guide.notesTitle: NTSA Smart Driving License Classes (A–G), TIMS Fees & Endorsement Guide
overview: Under the Traffic Act (Cap 403) and NTSA Smart Driving License regulations, Kenya categorizes motor vehicle drivers into seven harmonized classes (Classes A through G) aligned with East African Community (EAC) standards. Every driver must transition from a Provisional Driving License (PDL) through an accredited driving school, pass the NTSA theory and practical yard/road test, and obtain a biometric chip-embedded Smart Driving License via the eCitizen TIMS portal.

Commercial truck drivers (Class C), public service matatu/bus drivers (Class D), and commercial motorcycle couriers (Class A2/A3) must meet strict age and experience progression intervals before endorsing higher classes.
howItWorks: Switch between the License Classes (A–G), Application Process, and Official NTSA Fee Schedule tabs.
Check the minimum statutory age, maximum vehicle weight/passenger capacity, and prerequisite years of driving experience required for each class.
Follow the 6-step eCitizen TIMS workflow for PDL issuance, test booking, biometric capture, and 1-year vs. 3-year Smart DL renewal.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Total Statutory Cost to Obtain a Class B (Light Vehicle) Smart DL
workedExample.scenario: A first-time learner driver applying for a Class B1/B2 (Automatic or Manual Saloon/SUV) driving license via eCitizen:
steps: 1. Provisional Driving License (PDL — valid 3 months): KES 650
2. Driving Test Booking Fee (NTSA Theory & Practical Examination): KES 1,050
3. Biometric Smart Driving License (3-Year Validity): KES 3,050
Total Official NTSA / eCitizen Statutory Fees: KES 4,750 (excluding driving school tuition of KES 12,000–18,000)
workedExample.takeaway: Choosing a 3-year Smart DL renewal (KES 3,050) instead of three separate 1-year renewals saves time and repeated eCitizen convenience fees.

complianceTips: To qualify for a Class D1/D2 PSV endorsement (Matatu or Bus), a driver must be at least 22 years old, hold a Class B license for at least 3–4 years, and hold a valid NTSA PSV Badge.
Driving with an expired license or operating a vehicle class not endorsed on your Smart DL attracts an instant NTSA fine of KES 3,000 to KES 10,000.
notes: Select a driving license category (Class A motorcycles, Class B light vehicles, Class C commercial trucks, Class D PSVs, or Class G industrial equipment) to view NTSA age, endorsement, and upgrade rules.
Review step-by-step eCitizen TIMS application procedures from Provisional Driving License (PDL) enrollment through theory/practical testing to Smart Driving License collection.
Fee schedules reflect published National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) citizen service rates.

faq.question: How do I get a driving license in Kenya?
faq.answer: The process involves: 1. Getting a medical check (DL Form 1), 2. Enrolling in an NTSA-approved driving school, 3. Getting a provisional license (PDL), 4. Passing a theory test, 5. Passing a practical driving test, and finally 6. Paying for and collecting your license.

faq.question: What is the age limit for a driving license in Kenya?
faq.answer: You must be at least 18 years old for Class A (motorcycles), Class B (cars), and Class G (tractors). For Class C (heavy vehicles) you must be 21, for Class BCE (trailers) you must be 24, and for driving instructors you must be 25.

faq.question: How much does a driving license cost in Kenya?
faq.answer: The NTSA Smart Driving Licence fee is KES 3,050 and it is valid for 3 years. The total cost including driving school fees, medical checks, provisional licenses, and test fees varies by class and provider; confirm the payable amount in eCitizen.

faq.question: How long is a Kenyan driving license valid?
faq.answer: The NTSA Smart Driving Licence is valid for 3 years from the date of issue. The current renewal fee is KES 3,050; confirm the amount in eCitizen before payment.

faq.question: Do I need a new Smart Driving License?
faq.answer: Yes, NTSA is phasing out the old red booklet licenses. All new applications and renewals are issued as the new digital Smart Driving License card, which contains a microchip with your driver profile and demerit points.

traffic-fines.notesTitle: Kenya Traffic Act (Cap 403) Offences, Minor Fines & Demerit Points Guide
overview: Road traffic enforcement in Kenya is governed by the Traffic Act (Cap 403), the NTSA (Operation of Public Service Vehicles) Regulations, and the scheduled Minor Traffic Offences statutory notice. Under Kenyan law, scheduled minor traffic offences carry fixed statutory fines (ranging from KES 500 to KES 10,000) payable exclusively through official government digital channels or court cash bail, while serious offences (such as drunk driving, causing death by dangerous driving, or operating an unroadworthy vehicle) require mandatory court appearance.
Knowing the exact statutory fine for each offence protects motorists, boda boda riders, and PSV crews from roadside extortion and unlawful vehicle impoundment.

workedExample.takeaway: PSV matatus, buses, and commercial trucks are legally speed-governed at 80 km/h in Kenya—tampering with a speed governor carries heavy fines and immediate suspension of the vehicle's TLB/NTSA inspection sticker.

complianceTips: Never pay cash bribes at a police check—all legitimate traffic fines are paid via the Judiciary e-Filing / KCB court cash bail PayBill or eCitizen NTSA portal with an official receipt.
Accumulating 12 or more demerit points on your Smart Driving License within 24 months triggers mandatory license suspension under NTSA regulations.

Minor traffic fines are payable strictly through official eCitizen / NTSA digital channels or designated court registries—never pay unreceipted cash bribes on the road.

faq.question: What is the fine for speeding in Kenya?
faq.answer: Speeding fines range from KES 5,000 for exceeding the limit by up to 10 km/h, to KES 50,000 for exceeding by over 40 km/h. Higher speed offences also carry more demerit points and may result in arrest.

faq.question: What is the NTSA demerit points system?
faq.answer: Kenya uses a 24-point demerit system over a 3-year period. Points 1–12 result in a warning, 13–18 require a mandatory road safety course, 19–23 lead to license suspension for 6 months, and 24+ points result in license revocation.

faq.question: What is the fine for driving without insurance in Kenya?
faq.answer: Driving without valid motor vehicle insurance carries a fine of up to KES 50,000 and is an arrestable offence. You can also face imprisonment. Insurance is a legal requirement under Cap 405.

faq.question: How do I pay NTSA traffic fines?
faq.answer: You can pay via: cash bond at the police station, M-Pesa paybill (NTSA service), eCitizen portal (ntsa.go.ke), or through court-imposed fine after a hearing.

faq.question: What is the fine for drunk driving in Kenya?
faq.answer: First offence DUI carries a fine of KES 100,000 plus license suspension for 1 year or imprisonment up to 2 years. Repeat offenders face KES 200,000 fine plus license revocation and up to 3 years imprisonment.

national-parks-directory.notesTitle: Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) 2026 Park Entry Fees & Safari Planning Guide

Entry tariffs are structured into three residency tiers—East African Citizens (KES), Kenyan Residents (KES), and Non-Residents (USD)—and by park classification (Premium Parks, Wilderness Parks, Urban/Scenic Parks, and Marine Parks).
All KWS park gates operate on a strictly cashless basis via the eCitizen / KWSPay portal, requiring visitors to book and pay for passenger and vehicle entry permits prior to arrival.

faq.question: How much does it cost to enter a national park in Kenya?
faq.answer: Entry fees vary by park and visitor category. Kenyan citizens pay KES 200–500/day, residents KES 400–2,500/day, and non-residents USD 15–90/day. Children pay approximately half. Premium parks like Maasai Mara and Amboseli charge more.

faq.question: What is the difference between a national park and a national reserve?
faq.answer: National parks are managed by Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) with no human settlement or grazing allowed. National reserves are managed by county governments and may allow some pastoral activities.

faq.question: What is the Big Five?
faq.answer: The Big Five are: Lion, Leopard, Elephant, Rhinoceros, and Cape Buffalo. The best parks to see all five include Maasai Mara, Lake Nakuru, and Ol Pejeta Conservancy.

faq.question: When is the best time for safari in Kenya?
faq.answer: The dry season (June–October) is best for wildlife viewing as animals gather around water sources. The Great Wildebeest Migration crosses into Maasai Mara from July–October. However, the green season (November–May) offers lower rates and fewer crowds.

faq.question: How do I book a KWS park visit?
faq.answer: You can book through the eCitizen portal (ecitizen.go.ke) or pay at the gate. For popular parks, advance booking is recommended, especially during peak season (July–October and December–January).

crop-planting-calendar.notesTitle: KALRO Agro-Ecological Zone Crop Planting & Harvest Calendar Guide
overview: Successful crop production in Kenya depends on aligning land preparation, certified seed selection, and basal fertilizer application with the onset of the bimodal rainfall seasons—the Long Rains (March–May, 'Masika') and Short Rains (October–December, 'Vuli')—across Kenya's seven diverse agro-ecological zones defined by the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO).

Planting maize, beans, potatoes, sorghum, or horticultural crops even two weeks after the onset of effective rains can reduce grain yields by 15% to 30% due to missed nitrogen mineralization (the 'Birch effect') and terminal moisture stress during flowering.

Top-Dressing (at knee-high / 4–5 weeks): 1 bag (50kg) of CAN per acre
workedExample.takeaway: Intercropping maize with nitrogen-fixing legumes (beans, cowpeas, or dolichos lablab) suppresses weeds, fixes atmospheric nitrogen, and provides an early food harvest after 75–90 days.

complianceTips: Always verify the KEPHIS scratch-off sticker on seed packets by sending the code via SMS to 1393 to confirm seed authenticity and germination certification.
In acidic highland soils (pH < 5.5), apply agricultural lime or use NPK 23:23:0 instead of DAP to prevent phosphorus lock-up.

faq.question: When should I plant maize in Kenya?
faq.answer: For the Long Rains season, plant maize in March–April in most regions. For Short Rains, plant in October (Nyanza, Coast, Eastern). Highland areas like the Rift Valley typically only have one season.

faq.question: What is intercropping and why is it recommended?
faq.answer: Intercropping means growing two or more crops together in the same field. The classic Kenyan example is maize + beans. Benefits include better soil fertility (legumes fix nitrogen), reduced pest pressure, and diversified income.

faq.question: Where can I get certified seeds in Kenya?
faq.answer: Buy from KEPHIS-registered seed dealers, Kenya Seed Company outlets, or licensed agrovets. Always check the KEPHIS certification label on the packet for germination guarantee.

faq.question: What are Kenya's two farming seasons?
faq.answer: Kenya has two main seasons: the 'Long Rains' (March–May) and 'Short Rains' (October–December). However, highland and western regions may have slightly different timing, and some areas only support one season.

faq.question: How do I know which crops suit my area?
faq.answer: Consider your altitude, annual rainfall, and soil type. Contact your local KALRO research station or county agricultural extension officer for personalized advice.

faq.question: How do I register for subsidized fertilizer in Kenya?

faq.question: How much cheaper is subsidized fertilizer?
faq.answer: Subsidized DAP costs approximately KES 2,500 per 50kg bag vs KES 5,500+ at market prices — a saving of over 50%. CAN is KES 1,800 subsidized vs KES 4,000 at market price.

faq.question: Which fertilizer should I use for maize?
faq.answer: Use DAP or NPK 23-23-0 at planting (for phosphorus and root development), then top-dress with CAN or Urea when the maize is knee-high (for nitrogen and vegetative growth).

faq.question: What affects livestock prices in Kenya?
faq.answer: Prices vary by animal condition/weight, breed, season (prices spike before Eid, Christmas, Easter), drought conditions (supply increase = lower prices), and market location.

faq.question: Where is the biggest livestock market in Kenya?
faq.answer: Dagoretti Market in Nairobi is the largest urban livestock market. For pastoral areas, Garissa and Isiolo are major trading hubs.

faq.question: How do I sell livestock at a market?
faq.answer: Bring your animals to the market on designated market days. You'll need a livestock movement permit from your local veterinary officer. Buyers negotiate directly with sellers.

mjengo-construction-calculator.notesTitle: Kenya Mjengo (House Construction) Bill of Quantities & BORAQS Cost Guide (2026)
overview: Building a residential home ('mjengo') in Kenya requires accurate estimation of both structural materials—machine-cut quarry stones ('mawe' in 9×9, 6×9, or 4×9 sizes), 50kg cement bags (32.5N and 42.5N), river sand, ballast, deformed high-yield steel reinforcement bars (Y8, Y10, Y12, Y16), and gauge 28/30 roofing sheets ('mabati')—and total turnkey construction costs per square metre.

Our Mjengo Calculator combines empirical Kenyan Quantity Surveying (QS) material take-off ratios with regional cost-per-square-metre benchmarks published by the Board of Registration of Architects and Quantity Surveyors (BORAQS), the Architectural Association of Kenya (AAK), and the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) Construction Input Price Index.
howItWorks: Select your construction region (Nairobi & Kiambu, Mombasa & Coast, Kisumu & Western, Nakuru & Rift Valley, or Mt. Kenya & Eastern) to load localized material prices.

Choose a house preset (2-Bedroom Bungalow, 3-Bedroom Bungalow, 4-Bedroom Maisonette, or 5-Bedroom Villa) or enter your exact plinth area in square metres (m²) and finish tier (Standard, Middle-Income, or Luxury).
Inspect the complete Bill of Quantities (BoQ) material breakdown and the 6-stage budget allocation from Substructure (Foundation) to Finishes.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: 3-Bedroom Bungalow (130 m² Plinth Area, Standard Finish in Nairobi/Kiambu)
workedExample.scenario: Estimating materials and turnkey cost for a 130 m² single-storey 3-bedroom house:
steps: Turnkey Construction Cost (130 m² × ~KES 42,500/m² Standard Finish): ~KES 5,525,000
Machine-Cut Stones (6×9 & 9×9 external/internal walling + foundation): ~6,800 – 7,500 stones
Cement (50kg bags across foundation, slab, mortar & plaster): ~520 – 580 bags
River Sand: ~72 tonnes · Ballast (3/4 inch): ~55 tonnes · Deformed Steel Bars (Y10/Y12/Y8): ~185 bars
Roofing Sheets (Gauge 28 Box Profile / Versatile Mabati + Timber/Steel Trusses): ~165 – 185 sheets
workedExample.takeaway: In Kenyan residential construction, raw materials account for roughly 65%–70% of the budget while skilled and unskilled fundi labour accounts for 30%–35%.

complianceTips: Projects exceeding statutory thresholds must be registered with the National Construction Authority (NCA) using an NCA-licensed contractor, along with County Government architectural & structural plan approvals and NEMA environmental screening.
Always buy KEBS-certified cement (CEM IV/B 32.5N for general masonry/plaster and CEM I 42.5N for suspended slabs, columns, and structural beams) and BS 4449 certified steel bars.
notes: Enter your target floor area (square metres), building typology (bungalow, maisonette, apartments, or commercial perimeter wall), finish standard, and Kenyan region to estimate total construction cost.

Inspect itemized bill-of-quantities (BQ) estimates for substructure, superstructure walling (machine-cut quarry stone vs. interlocking blocks), roofing, electrical/plumbing, and finishes alongside material quantities (bags of cement, tonnes of steel, sand, and ballast).
Unit rates are calibrated against the Architectural Association of Kenya (AAK) and Institute of Quantity Surveyors of Kenya (IQSK) building cost handbook.

faq.question: Should I buy machine-cut Ndarugo stone or hand-dressed quarry stone?
faq.answer: Machine-cut stones (9x9) cost slightly more per piece (KES 45–55) than hand-dressed stones (KES 32–42), but use 35% less mortar and require much thinner plaster coats.

faq.question: Are residential houses exempt from the NCA construction levy?
faq.answer: Projects receive county architectural/structural plan approvals and NCA registration; always use an NCA-registered contractor and licensed structural engineer.

trademark-cost-kenya.notesTitle: KIPI Trademark (Classes 1–45), Patent & KECOBO Copyright Registration Guide
overview: Protecting your brand name, logo, software, invention, or creative work in Kenya is governed by two primary state agencies: the Kenya Industrial Property Institute (KIPI) under the Trade Marks Act (Cap 506) and Industrial Property Act (2001) for Trademarks, Patents, Utility Models, and Industrial Designs, and the Kenya Copyright Board (KECOBO) under the Copyright Act (Cap 130) for literary, musical, artistic, audio-visual, and software works.

Registering a trademark with KIPI grants you 10 years of renewable exclusive statutory rights across Kenya under the International Nice Classification (Classes 1–34 for Goods and Classes 35–45 for Services), enabling you to block counterfeits via the Anti-Counterfeit Authority (ACA).
howItWorks: Select the Intellectual Property right you wish to register: Trademark (KIPI), Patent (KIPI), Utility Model, Industrial Design, or Copyright (KECOBO).

For Trademarks, specify the number of Nice Classification classes (1 to 45) to compute the exact statutory fees across Preliminary Search (TM 27), Application Filing (TM 2), KIPI Journal Advertisement, and Registration Certificate (TM 11).
Compare official statutory government fees for Kenyan citizens/SMEs across each stage of the registration lifecycle.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Registering a Brand Logo in 1 Nice Class at KIPI (Kenyan Applicant)
workedExample.scenario: A Kenyan startup registers its brand name and logo in Class 35 (Retail & Business Services) directly at KIPI:
steps: Stage 1 — Preliminary Availability Search (Form TM 27, optional but recommended): KES 3,000
Stage 2 — Application to Register a Trademark in 1st Class (Form TM 2): KES 4,000
Stage 3 — Advertisement in the KIPI Industrial Property Journal (60-day opposition window): KES 3,000
Stage 4 — Issuance of Certificate of Registration (Form TM 11, valid 10 years): KES 2,000
Total Statutory KIPI Government Fees (1 Class): KES 12,000 (KES 9,000 if skipping TM 27 search)
workedExample.takeaway: Each additional Nice Class filed within the same trademark application costs slightly less than a standalone first-class filing—always cover both your product class and your retail/service class.

complianceTips: Once a trademark is examined and approved, it must be advertised in the monthly KIPI Journal for 60 days to allow third-party opposition before the final certificate is issued.
Software code, mobile apps, books, and music are registered online via the KECOBO National Rights Registry (NRR) portal on eCitizen for KES 1,000 per work.
notes: Select applicant residency status (Kenyan Citizen/Local Entity vs. Foreign Applicant) and number of Nice Classification classes (1 to 45) to calculate official Kenya Industrial Property Institute (KIPI) trademark registration fees.

Review stage-by-stage statutory fees from preliminary TM27 search and TM2 application filing through Industrial Property Journal advertisement (60-day opposition window) to 10-year registration certificate issuance.
Fee schedules reflect the Industrial Property Act and gazetted KIPI tariff regulations.

faq.question: How much does it cost to register a trademark in Kenya?
faq.answer: The total KIPI fees for registering a trademark in one class are approximately KES 22,450. This includes search (KES 1,000), application (KES 3,850), examination (KES 5,500), Gazette publication (KES 3,300), registration (KES 7,700), and certificate (KES 1,100). Attorney fees are separate.

faq.question: How long does trademark registration take in Kenya?
faq.answer: Trademark registration typically takes 12–18 months from application to certificate issuance. This includes the 60-day opposition period after Gazette publication.

faq.question: What are trademark classes?
faq.answer: The Nice Classification divides goods and services into 45 classes (34 goods, 11 services). You need to register in each class relevant to your business. Each additional class costs KES 3,080 on top of the base application fee.

faq.question: What is the difference between a patent and a utility model?
faq.answer: A patent protects novel inventions for 20 years and requires thorough examination (costs ~KES 34,650). A utility model (petty patent) is simpler, faster (6–12 months), cheaper (~KES 13,750), but only lasts 10 years and has a lower inventiveness threshold.

faq.question: Do I need an IP attorney?
faq.answer: While not strictly required for Kenyan nationals, using a registered IP agent/attorney is highly recommended. They handle the technical filing process and respond to KIPI queries. Foreign applicants must use a registered Kenyan IP agent.

professional-bodies-kenya.notesTitle: Kenya Statutory Professional Regulatory Boards & License Verification Guide
overview: In Kenya, practicing a regulated profession—such as medicine, law, engineering, accounting, architecture, quantity surveying, pharmacy, nursing, teaching, or real estate agency—without a valid current practicing certificate from the relevant statutory board is a criminal offence under the respective Act of Parliament.

Our directory consolidates 24 statutory professional regulatory councils and boards in Kenya, providing their enabling legislation, initial registration fees, annual practicing renewal fees, academic admission requirements, and direct links to their public practitioner verification portals.
howItWorks: Search by profession (e.g., Doctor, Advocate, Engineer, CPA Accountant, Architect, Contractor, Pharmacist, Teacher), board name, or acronym (KMPDC, LSK, EBK, ICPAK, BORAQS, NCA, TSC, PPB).
Inspect initial registration fees, annual practicing license renewal costs, and mandatory CPD (Continuing Professional Development) requirements.
Click the official verification portal link to confirm whether a practitioner is in good standing for the current calendar year.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: How to Verify a Doctor, Lawyer, Engineer, or Architect Before Hiring
workedExample.scenario: Protecting yourself or your business from unqualified quacks before signing a contract or undergoing treatment:
steps: Medical Doctors & Clinics: Check the KMPDC Master Register at kmpdc.go.ke or send an SMS with the doctor's name/registration number to 20547.
Advocates / Lawyers: Search the Law Society of Kenya (LSK) Advocate Search Portal at online.lsk.or.ke to confirm an active 2026 Practicing Certificate.
Professional Engineers: Check the Engineers Board of Kenya (EBK) register at ebk.go.ke (Graduate Engineers cannot stamp structural drawings—only Registered Professional/Consulting Engineers can).
Architects & Quantity Surveyors: Verify active registration on the BORAQS portal (boraqs.or.ke).
workedExample.takeaway: Holding a university degree alone does not authorize a professional to practice independently in Kenya—they must hold a current annual Practicing Certificate from their statutory board.

complianceTips: Most Kenyan professional boards run a January 1 to December 31 practicing year and require 20 to 40 Continuing Professional Development (CPD) points annually prior to renewal.
Always ask for a practitioner's registration number and cross-check it on the official board portal before paying professional retainers.
notes: Search Kenya's statutory professional regulatory bodies and licensing councils by profession, acronym (LSK, KMPDC, EBK, ICPAK, BORAQS, NCK, PPB, TSC, EARB), or enabling Act of Parliament.
Compare initial registration fees, annual practicing certificate renewal costs, academic qualification requirements, and direct links to official online practitioner verification registers.
Always verify a practitioner's current annual license status on the regulator's portal before engaging professional legal, medical, engineering, or financial services.

faq.question: How do I verify if a professional is registered in Kenya?
faq.answer: Each regulatory body has a public register or verification portal. Use the verification URL provided for each body in our directory. For doctors, check kmpdc.go.ke; for lawyers, check lsk.or.ke/find-a-lawyer.

faq.question: Is professional registration mandatory in Kenya?
faq.answer: Yes, practising a regulated profession without valid registration is a criminal offence under the respective Acts. This applies to doctors, lawyers, engineers, accountants, nurses, and many other professions.

faq.question: How much does professional registration cost?
faq.answer: Costs vary widely — from KES 1,000 (TSC for teachers) to KES 20,000+ (CMA for investment advisors). Most bodies charge KES 3,000–10,000 for initial registration plus annual renewal fees.

passport-id-fees.notesTitle: Kenya e-Passport (34/50/66-Page), Maisha Namba ID & Civil Registration Guide (2026)
overview: Applications for Kenyan East African Community (EAC) biometric e-Passports, National Identity Cards (Maisha Namba), Birth Certificates, and Death Certificates are processed digitally through the eCitizen portal by the Directorate of Immigration Services and the Civil Registration Services (CRS) under the Ministry of Interior and National Administration.

Following the 2024/2026 gazetted fee revisions, knowing the exact page count tariff (A-Series 34-page, B-Series 50-page, or C-Series 66-page), replacement penalties for lost/mutilated passports, and required supporting documents prevents application rejections at Nyayo House or regional immigration offices.
howItWorks: Compare official 2026 gazetted fees across 34-page, 50-page, and 66-page Kenyan e-Passports, Diplomatic Passports, Lost/Mutilated replacements, National IDs, and Civil Registration certificates.
Review the mandatory document checklist (original ID, birth certificate, parents' IDs, recommender details, and old passport for renewals).
Locate the 8 regional Directorate of Immigration biometric capture stations (Nairobi Nyayo House, Mombasa, Kisumu, Nakuru, Eldoret, Embu, Kisii, and Kericho) plus diaspora embassies.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Choosing Between a 34-Page (A-Series) and 50-Page (B-Series) e-Passport
workedExample.scenario: An applicant on eCitizen comparing the 10-year cost of an A-Series vs. B-Series Kenyan e-Passport:
steps: 34-Page Ordinary e-Passport (A-Series, valid 10 years): KES 7,500
50-Page Ordinary e-Passport (B-Series, valid 10 years): KES 9,500 (only KES 2,000 extra for 16 additional visa pages)
66-Page Frequent Traveller e-Passport (C-Series, valid 10 years): KES 12,500
Lost Passport Replacement Fee: KES 20,000 (requires a Police Abstract and sworn Affidavit) · Mutilated Passport Replacement: KES 10,000
workedExample.takeaway: Because Kenyan e-Passports cannot have extra pages stitched in once full, frequent regional or international travellers save money by selecting the 50-page (KES 9,500) or 66-page (KES 12,500) booklet upfront.

complianceTips: All passport applications and fee payments are completed strictly online via ecitizen.go.ke—never pay middlemen or brokers outside Nyayo House.
First-time National ID registration for Kenyan youths turning 18 is KES 300 (or free during gazetted registration drives), while replacing a lost ID costs KES 1,000.
notes: Filter official Directorate of Immigration and Citizen Services fees by document category: e-Passports (34-page A Series, 50-page B Series, 66-page C Series), Maisha Namba / National ID cards, Civil Registration (Birth & Death Certificates), and Foreign National permits.
Review required supporting documents, biometric booking procedures on eCitizen, and standard processing timelines at Nyayo House and regional Huduma Centres.
All statutory payments must be completed exclusively through the official eCitizen gateway (ecitizen.go.ke).

faq.question: How much is a new passport in Kenya?
faq.answer: Passport fees vary by passport type and the current Immigration fee schedule. See the fee table above and confirm the amount shown in eCitizen before payment.

faq.question: How long does it take to get a Kenyan passport?
faq.answer: The official processing time is 10–15 working days after biometric capture. However, wait times can sometimes be longer depending on backlog. An expedited/emergency passport takes 1–3 days.

faq.question: How much does it cost to replace a lost National ID?
faq.answer: Replacement of a lost or damaged National ID is currently free under the government fee waiver. A lost ID still requires a police abstract, while a damaged ID should be surrendered. Confirm the waiver is still active before applying.

faq.question: How do I apply for a passport in Kenya?
faq.answer: The entire process starts online via the eCitizen portal. You fill out the application, pay the fees, and book an appointment. Then you visit the Immigration office or Huduma Centre on your appointment date with original documents for biometrics.

faq.question: Can I get a passport for my child?
faq.answer: Yes, Kenyan citizens under 18 can apply for a passport through eCitizen. The application must be made with a parent or legal guardian and the current fee should be confirmed in eCitizen before payment.

kenya-customs-restricted-items.notesTitle: KRA Customs Traveller Guide: Duty-Free Allowances, Permits & Prohibited Goods
overview: Passengers arriving at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA), Moi International Airport (Mombasa), Eldoret International Airport, or land border posts (Busia, Malaba, Namanga, Isebania, Lunga Lunga, Moyale) are subject to baggage inspection by the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) Customs & Border Control Department under the East African Community Customs Management Act (EACCMA, 2004).

Understanding the legal distinction between Duty-Free Personal Allowances (Green Channel), Restricted Goods requiring prior regulatory permits (Red Channel), and strictly Prohibited Contraband prevents airport confiscation, heavy customs fines, and prosecution.
howItWorks: Search for any item you plan to carry into or out of Kenya (e.g., drone, laptop, phone, alcohol, currency, seeds, pets, cosmetics, or electronics).
Review the 4 official KRA Customs categories: Strictly Prohibited Items, Restricted Items (Permit Required), Duty-Free Personal Allowances, and Currency Declaration Rules.
Identify the exact Kenyan regulatory agency (KCAA, CA, KEPHIS, PPB, KWS, or FRC) that issues import clearance permits prior to travel.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Bringing Electronics, Gifts & Cash Through JKIA Customs
workedExample.scenario: A passenger arriving at JKIA Nairobi from Dubai or London with personal luggage, gifts, a camera drone, and USD 12,000 in cash:
steps: Personal Duty-Free Allowance: Non-commercial personal gifts/items up to USD 500 (~KES 65,000), plus 1 litre of spirits (or 2 litres of wine), 250ml of perfume, and 200 cigarettes for passengers aged 18+.

Camera Drone (Unmanned Aircraft): Strictly RESTRICTED—without a prior import permit from the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA), customs officers will detain the drone at JKIA against a seizure receipt until KCAA clearance is obtained.

Cash exceeding USD 10,000: Carrying USD 12,000 is legal, but MUST be declared on the KRA Currency Declaration Form (Form F88) at the Red Channel under the Proceeds of Crime and Anti-Money Laundering Act (POCAMLA).
workedExample.takeaway: Returning Kenyan residents who have lived abroad for over 12 months and are permanently relocating qualify for duty exemption on one personal motor vehicle (owned for 12+ months) and used household effects.

complianceTips: Single-use plastic carrier bags and duty-free plastic shopping bags are confiscated at Kenyan airports under the NEMA plastic ban.
Commercial quantities of phones, clothes, or cosmetics exceeding the USD 500 traveller allowance must be declared at the Red Channel and assessed for Import Duty, Excise, and 16% VAT.
notes: Search or filter import and export commodities by restriction status (Prohibited, Restricted—Permit Required, or Duty-Free Passenger Allowance) under the East African Community Customs Management Act (EACCMA).
Identify the exact regulatory agency issuing import/export clearance permits—such as KEBS, KEPHIS, Pharmacy and Poisons Board (PPB), Communications Authority (CA), or KWS.
Review passenger baggage duty-free thresholds before arriving at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA), Moi International Airport, or land border posts.

faq.question: What happens if I bring a prohibited item into Kenya?
faq.answer: Prohibited items are confiscated and destroyed by Customs. You may also face heavy fines, prosecution, or imprisonment depending on the item (e.g., narcotics, firearms).

faq.question: What is the duty-free allowance for visitors to Kenya?
faq.answer: Visitors can bring personal items, up to USD 500 worth of non-commercial goods, 1 litre of spirits or 2 litres of wine, and 200 cigarettes without paying duty. These must be for personal use only.

faq.question: Can I bring a drone into Kenya?
faq.answer: Drones are restricted items. You must obtain an import permit and authorization from the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) before bringing a drone into the country. Unauthorized drones will be confiscated at the airport.

faq.question: How much cash can I carry into or out of Kenya?
faq.answer: You can carry any amount of currency, but amounts exceeding USD 10,000 (or equivalent in KES/other currencies) MUST be declared at Customs upon arrival or departure.

faq.question: Which channel should I use at the airport?
faq.answer: Use the Green Channel if you have nothing to declare and your goods are within the duty-free allowances. Use the Red Channel if you have restricted items, commercial goods, or goods exceeding your duty-free allowance.

nhif-hospital-finder.notesTitle: SHA / SHIF Accredited Health Facilities (KEPH Levels 2–6) & Benefits Guide
overview: Under the Social Health Insurance Act (No. 16 of 2023), the Social Health Authority (SHA) replaced the former National Hospital Insurance Fund (NHIF) to administer three national healthcare funds: the Primary Healthcare Fund (PHCF, covering Level 2 dispensaries and Level 3 health centres funded by the Exchequer), the Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF, funded by a 2.75% gross salary contribution or means-tested household contribution covering Level 4–6 inpatient and specialist outpatient care), and the Emergency, Chronic and Critical Illness Fund (ECCIF).

Our directory enables Kenyan patients and families to search accredited Public, Faith-Based/Mission, and Private hospitals across all 47 counties by Kenya Essential Package for Health (KEPH) Level (Levels 2 through 6).
howItWorks: Search for accredited hospitals by facility name, county, or sub-county, or filter by KEPH Level (Levels 2–6) and ownership (Public, Private, Faith-Based).

Understand how KEPH facility levels determine referral pathways under SHA/SHIF—from Level 2/3 primary care to Level 4 sub-county hospitals, Level 5 county referral hospitals, and Level 6 national teaching and referral hospitals (KNH, MTRH, KUTRRH).
Check facility services and accreditation status before seeking non-emergency inpatient or specialist care.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: How the SHA / SHIF Referral Pathway Works Across Hospital Levels
workedExample.scenario: A contributor registered with SHA seeks outpatient and subsequent surgical inpatient care:
steps: Step 1 — Primary Care (KEPH Level 2 Dispensary or Level 3 Health Centre): Covered under the Primary Healthcare Fund (PHCF) with zero out-of-pocket co-pay for basic outpatient consultations, lab tests, and essential drugs.

Step 2 — Referral to Level 4, 5, or 6 Hospital: For surgical, maternity, dialysis, oncology, imaging (MRI/CT scan), or ICU care, the patient is referred to a contracted Level 4–6 hospital covered by SHIF and ECCIF.

Step 3 — Emergency Care: Under the Kenyan Constitution (Article 43) and SHA regulations, any emergency case must be stabilized at any Level 2–6 facility under the Emergency, Chronic and Critical Illness Fund.
workedExample.takeaway: Dial *147# or visit sha.go.ke to register yourself and your dependents (spouse and children) and select your primary care facility.

complianceTips: Salaried employees contribute 2.75% of gross monthly salary to SHIF (with a statutory minimum contribution of KES 300/month), which is fully tax-deductible before PAYE.
Non-salaried / informal sector households undergo automated means testing via *147# to determine their annual SHIF household contribution.
notes: Search or filter accredited healthcare facilities by county, KEPH hospital level (Level 2 Dispensary through Level 6 National Referral Hospital), ownership (Public, Faith-Based, or Private), and inpatient/outpatient services.
Verify facility accreditation under the Social Health Authority (SHA / SHIF) Primary Healthcare Fund and Social Health Insurance Fund.
Facility classifications follow the Kenya Master Health Facility List (KMHFL) and Social Health Authority empanelment records.

faq.question: What is NHIF accreditation?
faq.answer: NHIF accreditation means a hospital or clinic has been approved by the National Hospital Insurance Fund to provide healthcare services to NHIF members. Only accredited facilities can accept NHIF cover directly.

faq.question: What does hospital level mean in Kenya?
faq.answer: Kenya's health system has 6 levels: Level 1 (community), Level 2 (dispensary), Level 3 (health centre), Level 4 (sub-county hospital with surgery), Level 5 (county referral with specialists), Level 6 (national referral — KNH, MTRH).

faq.question: Can I use NHIF at a private hospital?
faq.answer: Yes, many private hospitals are NHIF-accredited. However, NHIF cover at private facilities may require a co-payment for services that exceed NHIF rebate limits.

faq.question: Has NHIF transitioned to SHA / SHIF?
faq.answer: Yes, the Social Health Authority (SHA) and Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF) officially replaced NHIF on October 1, 2024 under the Social Health Insurance Act 2023. Salaried employees contribute 2.75% of gross salary, and accredited Level 2–6 facilities provide outpatient and inpatient care.

faq.question: How do I check if my hospital is NHIF-accredited?
faq.answer: You can check at nhif.or.ke or call the NHIF toll-free line 0800 720 601. This tool also lists major accredited facilities across Kenya.

child-growth-schedule.notesTitle: Kenya MOH KEPI Child Immunization Schedule & WHO Growth Standards Guide
overview: The Kenya Expanded Programme on Immunization (KEPI), administered by the Ministry of Health (MOH) Division of National Vaccines and Immunization Programme, provides free, life-saving childhood vaccines at all public, faith-based, and accredited health facilities across Kenya. Recorded in the official Mother and Child Health (MCH) Handbook ('Kadi ya Kliniki'), the KEPI schedule protects infants against tuberculosis, polio, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b, pneumococcal pneumonia, rotavirus diarrhoea, measles-rubella, yellow fever, and malaria.

Alongside timely immunization, monthly weight-for-age tracking against World Health Organization (WHO) Child Growth Standards (0 to 60 months) enables early detection of stunting, wasting, or faltering growth.
howItWorks: Enter your child's current age in months (0 to 60 months) and select Boys or Girls to evaluate WHO weight-for-age reference bands.
Inspect the complete MOH KEPI Vaccination Schedule from Birth (BCG, OPV 0) through 6, 10, and 14 Weeks, 6 Months, 9 Months, and 18 Months.
Review age-appropriate motor, speech, and cognitive developmental milestones alongside nutrition guidance.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Key KEPI Clinic Visits in a Baby's First Year
workedExample.scenario: Tracking mandatory free MOH KEPI immunization visits from birth to 18 months:
steps: At Birth (or within 2 weeks): BCG (left forearm against TB) + Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV 0)
At 6, 10 & 14 Weeks: Pentavalent (DPT-HepB-Hib 1, 2, 3), PCV-10 (Pneumococcal 1, 2, 3), Rotavirus (at 6 & 10 weeks), OPV (1, 2, 3), and IPV (Injectable Polio at 14 weeks)
At 6 Months: Vitamin A Supplement (100,000 IU) + Malaria Vaccine Dose 1 (in endemic Lake Basin/Western counties)
At 9 Months & 18 Months: Measles-Rubella (MR 1 at 9 months, MR 2 booster at 18 months) + Yellow Fever (9 months in designated high-risk counties)
workedExample.takeaway: All KEPI schedule vaccines and Vitamin A supplements are 100% free of charge at all public dispensaries, health centres, and county hospitals across Kenya.

complianceTips: Keep the MOH Mother and Child Health Booklet ('Pink/Blue Clinic Card') safe—primary schools require proof of completed KEPI immunizations during PP1 admission.
Ministry of Health guidelines recommend 100% exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months (0–6 months) before introducing nutrient-dense complementary foods at 6 months.
notes: Enter your child's date of birth and select sex to generate a personalized vaccination timeline based on the Ministry of Health's Kenya Expanded Programme on Immunization (KEPI).
Track upcoming and completed vaccine visits from Birth (BCG, OPV 0) through 6, 10, and 14 weeks (Pentavalent, PCV-10, Rotavirus) up to 9 and 18 months (Measles-Rubella and Yellow Fever).
Compare expected weight-for-age benchmarks against World Health Organization (WHO) Child Growth Standards and review key developmental milestones.

faq.question: What is the KEPI schedule?
faq.answer: The Kenya Expanded Programme on Immunization (KEPI) is the Ministry of Health's official schedule of free, routine childhood vaccinations designed to protect children from preventable diseases like polio, measles, and tuberculosis.

faq.question: Are KEPI vaccines free in Kenya?
faq.answer: Yes, vaccines in the routine KEPI schedule are provided free of charge at all public health facilities and many private facilities (though private clinics may charge a small administration fee).

faq.question: What should I do if my child misses a vaccine?
faq.answer: Visit the nearest health facility as soon as possible. The nurses will advise on a 'catch-up' schedule to ensure your child gets the missed doses safely.

faq.question: Why does my child need Vitamin A?
faq.answer: Vitamin A supplementation (given every 6 months from age 6 months to 5 years) is critical for boosting immunity and preventing blindness. It significantly reduces the risk of severe illness from infections.

faq.question: How is child growth monitored?
faq.answer: Growth is monitored using the WHO Child Growth Standards. Regular weighing ensures your child is growing adequately. Consistently poor weight gain or sudden weight loss should be checked by a healthcare provider.

kenyan-food-nutrition.notesTitle: Kenya Food Composition Tables (MOH / KEMRI / FAO) & Meal Nutrition Guide
overview: Based on the official Kenya Food Composition Tables (KFCT) jointly published by the Ministry of Health (MOH), Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI), and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), our Kenyan Food Nutrition Guide provides verified macronutrient profiles—Calories (kcal), Protein (g), Carbohydrates (g), Fat (g), and Dietary Fibre (g) per 100g edible portion—for over 60 authentic Kenyan staples, indigenous vegetables, legumes, meats, fish, and street foods.

Unlike generic Western nutrition apps that lack entries for *ugali*, *githeri*, *omena*, *managu*, *terere*, *nduma*, *mukimo*, or *mutura*, this tool is calibrated specifically for Kenyan household diets and clinical dietetics.
howItWorks: Search for any Kenyan food (e.g., ugali, chapati, sukuma wiki, managu, omena, nyama choma, nduma, kamande, matoke) or filter by food group.
Click any column header (Calories, Protein, Carbs, Fat, or Fibre) to sort foods from highest to lowest nutrient density.
Use the per-100g figures to balance your plate according to the Ministry of Health Kenyan Healthy Plate model.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Comparing Two Classic Kenyan Meals (Per 100g Cooked Portion)
workedExample.scenario: Comparing a traditional Whole-Maize Ugali + Omena + Managu meal against White Chapati + Fried Beef:
steps: Whole-Grain Ugali (100g cooked): ~115 kcal, 2.7g protein, 24g carbs, 2.1g fibre (low glycemic index when made from unrefined 'posho' flour)
Sun-Dried Omena / Dagaa (100g): ~310 kcal, 53g–55g protein, rich in bioavailable calcium, iron, and omega-3 fatty acids
Cooked Managu / African Nightshade (100g): ~38 kcal, 4.3g protein, 3.6g fibre, high in iron and beta-carotene
White Layered Chapati (100g): ~295 kcal, 7.5g protein, 46g carbs, 9.2g fat
workedExample.takeaway: Traditional Kenyan indigenous greens (managu, terere, saga, kunde, mrenda) and small lake fish (omena) deliver 2× to 4× more micronutrients and protein per shilling than refined urban fast foods.

complianceTips: For diabetes and weight management, substitute sifted white maize meal with whole-grain ('Grade 2 / Kienyeji') posho flour, sorghum/millet ugali, or arrowroots (nduma).

Follow the MOH Healthy Plate rule: fill 50% of your plate with non-starchy vegetables (sukuma, cabbage, managu), 25% with protein (beans, kamande, omena, fish, eggs, or lean meat), and 25% with starch (ugali, rice, chapati, or matoke).
notes: Search traditional and everyday Kenyan foods (ugali, sukuma wiki, githeri, mukimo,omena, nyama choma, ndengu, chapati, managu, and matoke) to inspect macronutrient and micronutrient profiles per 100g serving.
Compare energy (kcal), protein, carbohydrates, dietary fiber, iron, calcium, and vitamin content across staples, legumes, leafy vegetables, and proteins.
Nutritional values are compiled from the Kenya Food Composition Tables (Ministry of Health / KALRO / FAO).

faq.question: What is the most nutritious Kenyan food?
faq.answer: Omena (small fish) is extremely nutritious, offering massive protein (55g/100g) and high calcium. Traditional dark leafy greens like managu, terere, and kunde are packed with iron, vitamins, and fibre compared to common cabbage or sukuma wiki.

faq.question: Are Kenyan staples healthy?
faq.answer: Yes, but portion control is key. Ugali, rice, and chapati provide excellent energy (carbs) but are calorie-dense. A healthy Kenyan plate should be half vegetables, quarter protein, and quarter staple.

faq.question: Why is Nyama Choma high in calories?
faq.answer: Nyama Choma (grilled meat, especially goat) is often fatty, which significantly increases its calorie count (fat has 9 calories per gram compared to 4 for protein/carbs). Leaner cuts or grilled chicken are lower-calorie alternatives.

kplc-token-calculator.notesTitle: KPLC Prepaid Electricity Token Tariff, EPRA Levies & Lifeline Band Guide (2026)
overview: Prepaid electricity tokens purchased from Kenya Power and Lighting Company (KPLC) via M-Pesa PayBill 888880 or *977# are priced according to the Retail Electricity Tariff Schedule approved by the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA). Many Kenyan households wonder why KES 1,000 buys different token units (kWh) at different times of the month—the reason is that KPLC uses cumulative monthly consumption bands (Lifeline DC1 vs. Domestic Ordinary DC2/DC3) combined with seven variable pass-through levies and 16% VAT.

Specifically, approximately 35% to 42% of every token purchase goes toward Fuel Energy Cost Charge (FCC), Foreign Exchange Rate Fluctuation Adjustment (FERFA), Inflation Adjustment (IA), WARMA Levy, EPRA Levy, Rural Electrification Programme (REP 5%), and 16% VAT before the remaining amount is divided by your base energy rate per kWh.
howItWorks: Enter the KES amount you plan to spend on KPLC prepaid tokens and select your customer tariff category (Domestic Lifeline 0–30 kWh, Domestic Ordinary 30–100 kWh / >100 kWh, or Small Commercial SC1).
Inspect the exact item-by-item deduction of base energy cost, Fuel Cost Charge, Forex Adjustment, Inflation Adjustment, REP (5%), EPRA/WARMA levies, and 16% VAT.
See the exact number of kWh units generated and your effective all-in cost per kWh.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: Why KES 1,000 Buys ~37.5 Units on Lifeline vs. ~26.8 Units on Domestic Ordinary
workedExample.scenario: Comparing a KES 1,000 token purchase under the Domestic Lifeline band (≤30 kWh/month) vs. Domestic Ordinary band (>30 kWh/month):
steps: Domestic Lifeline Tariff (DC1 — households consuming ≤30 kWh per calendar month): Base energy rate is ~KES 12.23/kWh (plus levies & VAT ≈ KES 26.60/kWh all-in) → KES 1,000 buys ~37.5 kWh (capped at 30 kWh/month).

Domestic Ordinary Tariff (DC2/DC3 — consumption above 30 kWh/month): Base energy rate rises to ~KES 19.03–20.97/kWh (plus FCC, FERFA, IA, 5% REP & 16% VAT ≈ KES 36.50–37.30/kWh all-in) → KES 1,000 buys ~26.8 to 27.4 kWh.
workedExample.takeaway: To stay within the subsidized Lifeline tariff (DC1), a household's total cumulative token purchases across 3 consecutive billing months must average 30 kWh or less per month.

complianceTips: There is NO time-of-month discount trick (buying on the 1st of the month does not give more units unless your meter qualifies for the monthly 0–30 kWh Lifeline band reset).
If your meter has an outstanding KPLC reconnection fee or token loan, KPLC deducts arrears first before converting the balance into kWh units.
notes: Enter your KPLC prepaid token purchase amount (KES) and select your customer tariff band (Domestic Lifeline DC1, Domestic Ordinary DC2/DC3, or Small Commercial SC) to estimate kilowatt-hours (kWh) received.

View a transparent itemization of every statutory surcharge deducted before energy units are calculated: Fuel Energy Cost Charge (FECC), Foreign Exchange Rate Fluctuation Adjustment (FERFA), Inflation Adjustment, WARMA & EPRA levies, Rural Electrification Programme (REP 5%), and 16% VAT.
Tariff bands and Pass-Through adjustment formulas follow Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) gazetted retail electricity schedules.

faq.question: How many KPLC units will I get for KES 1,000?
faq.answer: Under the EPRA 2023–2026 tariff structure, KES 1,000 buys approximately 38 kWh on the Lifeline tariff (DC1, 0–30 kWh/month) or ~31 kWh on the Domestic Ordinary tariff (DC2, 31–100 kWh/month) after Fuel Energy Cost, Forex Adjustment, EPRA/WRA/REP levies, and 16% VAT.

faq.question: What is the KPLC fixed charge of KES 150?
faq.answer: EPRA abolished the monthly KES 150 fixed standing charge for domestic prepaid customers under the 2023–2026 tariff review. Every shilling you pay goes directly toward energy units and per-unit statutory levies/VAT.

faq.question: What is the lifeline tariff?
faq.answer: Under the EPRA 2023–2026 tariff structure, the Domestic Lifeline band (DC1, 0–30 kWh/month) is charged at a base rate of KES 12.14/kWh. Ordinary Domestic DC2 (31–100 kWh) is KES 16.50/kWh, and DC3 (above 100 kWh) is KES 19.07/kWh, with no monthly fixed standing charge.

faq.question: What levies are included in KPLC token charges?
faq.answer: Each unit includes: Rural Electrification Levy (KES 0.12), REP Fund Levy (KES 0.03), EPRA Levy (KES 0.10), WARMA Levy (KES 0.03), Fuel Cost Charge (~KES 3.87), and Forex Adjustment (~KES 0.67). Plus 16% VAT on everything.

faq.question: Why do I get fewer units than the base tariff rate suggests?
faq.answer: Three main reasons: (1) once your cumulative monthly consumption crosses 30 kWh (Lifeline DC1) or 100 kWh (Domestic Ordinary DC2), your tariff steps up to a higher per-unit energy rate, (2) EPRA pass-through surcharges (Fuel Energy Cost Charge, Forex Adjustment, Inflation Adjustment, WARMA, EPRA, and 5% REP levy) are added to every unit, and (3) 16% VAT is charged on the taxable components.

water-bill-calculator.notesTitle: WASREB County Water & Sewerage Tiered Block Tariff Guide (2026)
overview: Urban water supply and sanitation services in Kenya are regulated by the Water Services Regulatory Board (WASREB) under the Water Act (2016) and delivered by County Water and Sanitation Companies—including Nairobi City Water and Sewerage Company (NCWSC), Mombasa Water (MAWASCO), Kisumu Water (KIWASCO), Nakuru Water (NAWASSCO), and Eldoret Water (ELDOWAS).

To ensure affordable basic water for low-income households while discouraging wastage, WASREB enforces an Increasing Block Tariff (IBT) structure: the first 0–6 cubic metres (m³, where 1 m³ = 1,000 litres) is billed at a subsidized lifeline rate, with progressively higher per-m³ rates across upper consumption blocks, plus a Sewerage Charge (typically 75% of the water bill for sewer-connected premises) and a KES 50 meter rent.
howItWorks: Select your County Water Utility (Nairobi NCWSC, Mombasa MAWASCO, Kisumu KIWASCO, Nakuru NAWASSCO, or Eldoret ELDOWAS).
Enter your monthly water consumption in cubic metres (m³ = current meter reading minus previous reading; 1 m³ = 1,000 litres) and toggle whether your property is connected to the county sewer line.
Review the block-by-block water charge, sewerage charge, meter rent, and total monthly payable bill.

workedExample.title: Worked Example: 15 m³ (15,000 Litres) Monthly Consumption on Nairobi Water (NCWSC)
workedExample.scenario: A sewer-connected household in Nairobi consumes 15 m³ of water in a month:
steps: Block 1 (Lifeline 0 – 6 m³): Covered at the minimum lifeline block rate
Block 2 (7 – 20 m³ = 9 m³ in this tier): Billed at the second residential block tariff per m³
Sewerage Charge (for properties connected to the public sewer network): 75% of the water consumption charge
Monthly Meter Rent: KES 50 (for a standard 1/2-inch domestic connection)
workedExample.takeaway: Fixing a single leaking toilet cistern (which can waste 10 to 15 m³ per month) prevents your household from crossing into the punitive >20 m³ and >50 m³ commercial tariff blocks.

complianceTips: 1 cubic metre (1 m³) equals exactly 1,000 litres (or fifty 20-litre 'mtungi' jerrycans).
Submit monthly self-meter readings via your county water utility's USSD code (e.g., *888# for Nairobi Water) to avoid estimated billing disputes.
notes: Select your county water and sewerage utility (e.g., Nairobi City Water & Sewerage Company, Mombasa Water, Eldowas, Kiwasco, Nakuru Water, or Mawasco) and enter your monthly water consumption in cubic metres (m³).
Compute your progressive block tariff water charge, sewerage surcharge (typically 75% of water bill where connected), meter rent, and WASREB regulatory levy.
Tariff blocks reflect Water Services Regulatory Board (WASREB) approved county water utility schedules.

faq.question: How is my water bill calculated in Kenya?
faq.answer: Water bills in Kenya use a step-function (block) tariff. You pay a lower rate for the first few cubic metres (lifeline tariff), and the rate increases as your consumption rises. A sewerage surcharge (typically 75% of the water charge) and fixed meter rent are added.

faq.question: What is the lifeline tariff?
faq.answer: The lifeline tariff is a subsidized rate for the first 0–6 cubic metres of water consumed per month. It ensures basic water access for low-income households at a very low cost (typically KES 33–45 per m³ under WASREB domestic tariff bands).

faq.question: How much water does an average Kenyan household use?
faq.answer: An average household of 4–5 people in Nairobi uses approximately 10–20 cubic metres (m³) per month. This covers cooking, cleaning, bathing, and laundry. Households with gardens or larger families may use 30+ m³.

faq.question: Why is there a sewerage charge?
faq.answer: The sewerage charge covers wastewater treatment and sewer network maintenance. It's calculated as a percentage (usually 75%) of your water consumption charge. Properties not connected to the sewer network may be exempt.

faq.question: Which body regulates water tariffs in Kenya?
faq.answer: The Water Services Regulatory Board (WASREB) approves all water and sewerage tariffs in Kenya. Individual water utilities (like NCWSC for Nairobi) propose tariffs, and WASREB approves them after public consultation.
